paragraphs.text: OF OUR FATHER AMONG THE SAINTS, THE BISHOP OF NYSSA: A REFUTATION OF THE VIEWS OF APOLINARIUS. A fitting preface to our discourse would be the voice of the Lord, which bids us beware of the false prophets, "who come to you," he says, "in sheep's clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves; by their fruits you will know them." The fruit, then, tells apart the true sheep from the destroyer of sheep, who slips unchallenged into the gathered flock under a gentle guise, and it brings into the open the hostile mouth hidden beneath the gentleness. So we ought to look for the fruits, both the good ones and the worse, by which the disguise of deceit is uncovered; for he says, "By their fruits you will know them." Now the good fruit of any teaching, in my judgment at least, is the increase of those who are being saved in the Church; [?]

[?] the flock, and spreads the vine to every side of the house, and plants around the Master's table those who come from the error of the wild olive, turning them into a new planting of olives, and lays the mystical rods in the sweet, drinkable stream of teaching, by which the flocks become prolific, so that Laban's holdings dwindle while Jacob's portion thrives and multiplies with marked offspring. If anyone shows fruit of this kind from his teaching (for the fruit, as has been said, is the increase of the truth), he is truly a prophet, speaking by the Spirit in keeping with the divine purpose. But suppose someone strips the shoots from the vine, leaves the divine table desolate by uprooting the planting, and plots against the spiritual watering-trough, so that the sheep no longer conceive by the patriarch's rods or multiply the flock with marked offspring, but are driven away from the nourishing pasture (that is, from the traditions of the fathers), and lodge outside the fold, and scatter to foreign pastures. When the fruit of teaching is of this kind, the wolfish form hidden under the sheep's skin becomes plain. Let us therefore examine what the teaching of Apolinarius the Syrian has produced for us: increase of the flocks or decrease, gathering of the scattered or breaking up of those who stood together, defense or overthrow of the doctrines of the fathers. If the zeal of the man in question looks toward the better, he is surely a sheep and not a wolf. But if the reverse, "Beware of the false prophets," says the Lord. Do not let that mouth escape notice. It is sharpened with the teeth of innovation to injure and destroy any body that comes near it, and it tears apart the healthy body of the Church of God. So that what I say may not seem to be mere abuse, we shall set out one of the treatises he has circulated, whose title is this: "A Demonstration," he says, "concerning the Divine Incarnation in the Likeness of Man." Perhaps someone who laid bare the sense of the title with precision would not need the treatise itself to expose the absurdity of the doctrine. "A Demonstration concerning the Divine Incarnation in the Likeness of Man." It would be better to set out the divine sayings to refute this new coinage of terms. "The Word," it says, "became flesh"; and, "Glory dwelt in our land"; and, "God was manifested in the flesh." Through each

of these sayings we may learn that the Divine, which is always unchangeable and unalterable in its essence, comes to be in the changeable and alterable nature, so as to heal our turning toward evil by its own unchangeableness. But this man does not say that God was manifested in the flesh. That would be the same as saying that the Word became flesh: the Word who, in the likeness and form of a man, lived among human beings by taking the form of a slave. Instead he invents a kind of "divine incarnation" of the Word, and I do not know what he means by the expression. Perhaps he means a change of the Godhead, altered from its simple and uncompounded nature into fleshly solidity. Or perhaps he means that the divine essence remained in itself while some other divine enfleshment appeared on the boundary between the nature of men and that of God, being neither man nor God but somehow sharing in both. In being an incarnation it would be akin to the human, and in being divine it would be higher than the human. Yet it cannot be God, for the Divine is simple and uncompounded by nature, and whatever is separated from simplicity is equally and wholly separated from Godhead. Nor again is it a man. What is made up of a rational soul and a body is called a man, and where the two are not conceived together, how will the name "man" fit? We speak of a man's body and of a man's soul as long as each is considered by itself, but the coming together of the two both is and is called a man. So what this "divine incarnation" is, being neither man nor God, which the title of the treatise fabricates, cannot be found from what we have examined. "A Demonstration," he says, "concerning the Divine Incarnation in the Likeness of Man." And what does this phrase "in the likeness of man" signify? That the divine incarnation is constituted in the same way as a human one. When did this happen? In the last days? Then where is the mystery of the virginity? For the Lord was not made flesh in the likeness of man, as the treatise-writer says, but by divine power and the Holy Spirit, as the Gospel says. Or was it before the ages? Then how can what is be made like what is not? Man is the last of the things in creation, but the Lord is king before the ages. In the likeness of what man, then, was that divine incarnation made in the time before the ages? [?]

For what is like is surely like something that exists, not like something that does not exist. So his argument contains two absurdities at once. Either the thing formed turns out to be older than the one who formed it, or the Divine, in becoming flesh, is made like what does not exist; for in the beginning the Godhead was, but Adam was not. Therefore, if the divine nature is made flesh in the likeness of man, the divine incarnation is made like what does not exist, and what is made like the non-existent would surely not exist itself. But he says that this incarnation came about in some way other than the human. Then what likeness can there be between things of different natures? It is impossible for the divine incarnation to have come about in the likeness of man before the ages. Nor could it do so at the end of the times, when the Lord's dispensation as man took place [?], by which God was manifested in the flesh, for the mystery of the virginity does not admit such a notion. Since neither is possible, he composed this title for his treatise in vain on either interpretation. That the title is ill-considered and rests on no coherent thought has, I think, been shown sufficiently by what has been said, at least to those who listen attentively. It would now be time to set out for examination the treatise itself that this title announces. I shall give its opening parts in my own words, running briefly through the sense, since here there is no risk in passing over some of what is written without examining it. "It was good," he says, "that only the pious faith be held [?]; for unexamined faith did not profit even Eve. So the faith of Christians too ought to be examined, lest it unawares fall in with the opinions of the Greeks or the Jews." After making this preface at greater length, he introduces his argument, saying: "Among unbelievers and among the heresies it has long been noised abroad that it is impossible for God to become man and to have to do with sufferings. This is also introduced among the heresies under the guise of faith, since they call Christ a God-inspired man on account of his birth from a woman and his sufferings." What heresies he knows of that call Christ a God-inspired man, he himself would know, and so would anyone schooled in his teachings. But we have visited many places and have eagerly discussed the questions concerning the Word both with those who share our doctrine and with those who have broken away from it, and we have never yet heard anyone utter such a statement about the mystery, that Christ was a

God-inspired man. Anyone who means to correct mistaken notions about the doctrine and to put more pious ones in their place ought not to fabricate things that do not exist and fight against what has no reality. He ought to arm himself against what his opponents actually say. Skilled physicians do not turn their art against diseases that do not exist; they set their science against an illness that is already present. So let him either produce someone who has said, not that God was manifested in the flesh, but that Christ is a God-inspired man, and then we shall accept that his treatise was not composed in vain; or, as long as no such disease is found, everyone will agree that it is futile to grapple with what does not exist. But it is not idly that he contrives this need to write. He wanted a road and a line of argument for establishing his own doctrine, and so he presented as already said something that no one had said. By seeming to contend against it, he could use his contrived refutation to establish that the Divine is mortal. The whole aim of his treatise looks to this: that the Godhead of the only-begotten Son is mortal, and that it was not the human element that received the suffering, but the impassible and unalterable nature was altered so as to share in suffering. What use the argument serves for him, those initiated into his mysteries would know. But what its logic shows even to mere infants is such as not even the most godless of the Greeks would say. For if the Godhead of the Only-begotten itself died, then surely life, truth, righteousness, goodness, light and power all died with it; for the only-begotten God both is and is called all these things under different aspects. Being simple, without parts and uncompounded, he is wholly whatever he is called, not this in one part and that in another. So where one of these is, all are understood to be in him, and where it is not, all are erased together. If, then, the Divine was annihilated by death, everything seen as joined to his Godhead was annihilated by death along with it. Yet Christ is not simply power, but the power of God and the wisdom of God. Since, then, it is confessed that these belong to the Godhead of the Son through [?]

the Father [?]. If, then, power was extinguished by death, and Christ is the power of God, what power in turn was called back from non-existence, when the existing power had been annihilated by death and no other was left? Even those who fight against us confess that the power of the Father is in the Son. If, then, there is one power, and it was overpowered by death and passed into annihilation at the time of the dispensation of the passion, what other power does he invent besides it, one that called this power back from death? If they should say that one power died while the other remained immortal, they will no longer confess that the Father's power is in the Son. And so, by consequence, they set aside the Lord's own words as untrue, the words that testify that all that is the Father's is the Son's. He who has all that is the Father's surely has the Father's immortality in himself as well. And immortality, as long as it is what it is called, has no mixture with death and no share in it. So if they say that the Godhead of the Son is mortal [?], they make out that he does not have the Father's immortality in himself. Yet the one who says that he has the whole Father in himself speaks the truth. So the man who makes mortal the one in whom the whole eternity of the Father is seen is lying. According to the account of the pious, the power of the Father and the Son is one, for in the Father we see the Son and in the Son the Father. It is therefore clearly shown that what is passible by nature receives death, while what is impassible [?]. But let us go on to the next part of the treatise. I shall again give it in my own words, summing up its sense briefly. He says that to call Christ a God-inspired man is contrary to the apostolic teachings and foreign to the synods, and that Paul, Photinus and Marcellus started this perversion. Then, like skilled combatants, as though he had come to grips with an opponent in debate and had found the author of the phrase, he says this: "How will you call a man from earth the one who is testified to have come down from heaven as a man, and is proclaimed Son of Man?" Here again, the case he built earlier becomes the beginning of another absurdity. In order to show that God died, he refuses to allow anything at all of earthly nature to be seen in him, since to [?]

[earthly nature] the suffering of death seems to be akin. "He is not," he says, "a man from earth, the man who came down from heaven." Yet he is a man, even if he has come down from heaven, for in the Gospels the Lord does not refuse that title. How then do you keep your statements consistent? If the man is not from earth but comes down to us from heaven, how is the one who comes down from heaven called Son of Man? On earth we think of fathers as coming before their sons. So he will surely have to grant that the man who on his view came from heaven is not named from a father for nothing, since he is called Son of Man. In his humanity, then, he must have another man in heaven, conceived of beforehand as his father. Suppose he relies on the saying, "No one has ascended into heaven except the one who came down from heaven, the Son of Man," and for this reason cuts him off from kinship with earthly man, calling the Son who came from heaven a man. Then he will surely have to grant that the one who came down to us has some other such father in heaven. In that case we would have to suppose that the heavenly life also has nations of men, peoples, and everything that exists in this life. If what came from heaven is a son of man, and what was born according to the flesh from Mary, of the seed of David, is named Son of Man from above [?], then on their view he is falsely called Son of God, since neither the heavenly nor the earthly is related to the Divine. But he gathers what has been said into a summary and concludes his argument with this: "If he is both Son of Man from heaven and Son of God from a woman, how is the same one not God and man?" I say that to believe the same one to be both man and God belongs to everyone who upholds right doctrine, but not in the sense the treatise-writer intends. The Divine is not earthly, nor is the heavenly human, as he supposes. Rather, from above the power of the Most High, through the Holy Spirit, overshadowed human nature, that is, was formed within it, while the undefiled Virgin contributed the portion of flesh. And so what was born of her was named Son of the Most High: the divine power claimed kinship with the Most High, and the flesh claimed kinship with humankind. "But he is God," he says, "by the spirit that was made flesh, and man by the flesh assumed by God." What, again, is the enfleshment of the spirit, apart from its union with our flesh? And from where was the man assumed, if not from the first man? Moses gives the genealogy of the first man, and we have heard from him that his first origin was from earth, not from heaven: "God took dust from the earth and formed man." But that another constitution of man

was established from heaven we have learned from no one. Then he adds to what he has said that "the mystery was manifested in the flesh." In saying this he speaks well; this is our own teaching. He also says that "the Word became flesh by union," and these too are the words of a sound voice. For whoever says that the Word was united to the flesh means nothing other than that the two came together. "But the flesh," he says, "is not soulless; for it is said to wage war against the spirit and to fight against the law of the mind." What splendid good sense! He does not wrap God in soulless flesh! Let us ask, then, whether God the Word assumed the flesh with a soul, as the treatise-writer says. We call the bodies of irrational animals ensouled too. Whoever joins human flesh to the Word, and ensouled flesh at that, joins nothing less than the whole man to him. The only distinctive mark of the human soul is its rational nature, since in everything else we share with the irrational animals. Desire, anger, appetite for food, fullness, sleep, digestion, assimilation, the excretion of what has become useless: all these are governed alike in us and in the irrational animals by a certain power of the soul. So whoever says that what was assumed was a man, and grants that it had a soul, has thereby borne witness that it also had the intellectual power proper to the human soul. This follows from the very words of the Apostle that he set before us. For the Apostle said, "The mind of the flesh is hostile to God; for it does not submit to the law of God." In saying this he plainly names the properties of the faculty of choice and thought. To be obedient or resistant to the law is proper to choice, and no one could separate the very word "mind" from the activity of thinking. Not even mere infants would deny that thinking is the same as understanding. And how could what fights against us and takes us captive lack the activity of the intellect? When the wicked have their will moved toward base things, that is no proof that there is no mind in them. They are without good understanding, but they think all the same. Even that serpent, which the Scriptures have taught us is the originator and inventor of evil, is not called mindless by the inspired word; it testifies that he was more shrewd than the others. So the very sayings he set before us, by which he thinks to establish his argument, expose the impiety of his doctrine. For it is not only in these words that the Apostle sets the flesh against the spirit, that is, the evil choice against [?] to fight against the law of the mind [?]

[?] … a more [?] life. And to the Corinthians too he says, reproaching them for their passions, "You are fleshly." Is it, then, that at the time when the word was addressed to them, the people concerned had no share in the activity of the mind, according to Apolinarius's threefold division of human beings? Or were they rather called fleshly by Paul because of their excessive attachment to the flesh, taking their name from what predominated in them? The context of what is written shows that this is the meaning: "For where there is jealousy and strife among you," he says, "are you not fleshly?" Yet jealousy and strife belong to the activity of the mind. What comes next in his treatise is meant to prove, by a good many testimonies, that a human being consists of three things: flesh, soul and mind. This is not far from our own view. It is the same thing to say that a human being is made of an intellectual soul and a body, and to count the mind separately by itself and so divide our account of the human being into three. It is true, though, that his argument here gives the heretics many handles. If one counts the intellective part by itself, one can say that the spirited part has another definition and the desiring part yet another. And perhaps someone who counted up the soul's remaining movements on the same principle would end up showing that a human being is many-sided and made of many parts, not three. But let this pass. We should not stretch our refutation beyond measure by going through every point. Let us go on to the next part of his argument. Having argued at length that the human compound is threefold, or tripartite, or whatever one cares to call it, he also mentions certain decrees of synods. One is from those assembled against Paul of Samosata, saying that the Lord was deified [?] from heaven. Another is the one pronounced at Nicaea, whose wording he quoted in these terms: "who came down from heaven, and was incarnate, and became man." Having said this, as if he had laid the groundwork for what he was about to say, he now lays bare what he really means. As if he were drawing a conclusion from what had been proved, he says in these very words: "Christ, then, having God as spirit, that is, as mind, together with soul and body, is fittingly called a man from heaven." What do these words have in common with what came before? Where [?] … for our salvation, having come down and been incarnate [?] …

… did the synod against the Samosatene decree this? But I pass over matters older than our knowledge. What did he show of this kind in the decrees of Nicaea? "Who came down from the heavens," the creed says, "and was incarnate." So the flesh is not to be thought of before the descent; it comes second, after the descent. This is proclaimed by everyone in the churches, "who was incarnate and became man," and this is our doctrine, or rather the Church's. Where, then, do these words say that "Christ, having God as spirit, that is, as mind, together with soul and body, is called a man from heaven"? Whether you examine the bare wording or the sense of what was said, you will find his claim in neither. The wording is as far from his wording as, in the Psalmist's phrase, the east is from the west. And what does the sense of those words have in common with what his words mean? He says that Christ, incarnate in human flesh, has God within himself as spirit, that is, as mind. And the man who says this is the very man who forbids us to call Christ a God-inspired man, having God within himself as one being within another, while he himself argues for exactly that more than anyone. The synod's statement says, "who came down from heaven." Let ordinary, simple people understand it as a descent from the heavens to us. We will not quarrel with that view, even though the mind may suggest a loftier meaning: that the Divine does not come down from place to place, since it is everywhere and holds all things in its grasp, and that the phrase points instead to its condescension to the lowliness of our nature. However one prefers to take the descent, the synod's statement then says "who was incarnate," and it is right to say this too. How could it have expressed the birth from a woman more fittingly? For as God he was not himself, in himself, born of a woman. He who exists before creation does not receive his very being by being born in the flesh. Rather, he prepared the way for the entry of his own power by the Holy Spirit. He needed no material starting point to build his own tent, but, as is said of Wisdom, "she built herself a house," he formed a man out of the dust taken from the Virgin, and through it he was blended with humanity. Where, then, do these words say what Apolinarius thinks: "Christ, having God as spirit, that is, as mind, together with soul and body, is fittingly called a man from

heaven"? If he may drag the divine oracles wherever he likes, and fit any meaning he pleases to the letter like an interpreter of dreams, then let him attach these and similar notions to the divine words. But the Apostle says that old wives' tales and profane, empty chatter must be rejected in every way. So he must on no account be allowed to join together things that have nothing in common or glue together things that do not fit. In fact, the very arguments he fights with in support of his claims would fight on our side, to overturn his doctrine. He says that Paul too calls the first Adam a soul, existing with a body, and in saying this he speaks rightly and in favor of the truth. Did the first man, then, whom Paul mentions as having become "a living soul," have some brutish and irrational soul? Yet the narrative testifies that he had no small gift of understanding. The animals were brought to him by God, and he had the authority to find their names, working out what was natural and fitting for each. Moreover, the disobedience, the inclination toward what ought not to be, the shame at what had been done, and the finding of a plausible defense against the charges are all proof of the mind's activity. Why, then, did Paul say nothing about the intellectual element of Adam's soul? Clearly because what is left out is named along with the part. So in "To you shall all flesh come," David means the whole human being by "flesh." And when Jacob went to live among the Egyptians with seventy-five souls, surely Scripture does not record that he was mindless or fleshless at that time? But the writer says that "the second man, from heaven, is called spiritual," and he makes this a sign that the man blended with God had no mind. Yet the refutation of this absurdity lies ready to hand in the very texts he cited. The one who said, "As is the heavenly one, so are those who are heavenly," takes us far away from any such notion. Those who have believed in him who came from heaven are themselves called heavenly by Paul, since they have moved their citizenship, as he puts it, to heaven. The Apostle says that as that heavenly one is, so are these heavenly ones too. And none of those who have accepted the faith is mindless. It is therefore entirely necessary that this comparison of likeness should prove that, in the likeness of human beings, the mind is in him as well. "As is the heavenly one," he says, "so are those who are heavenly." So they will have to admit that the mind is either in all of them or in none. For just as the properties of the earthly one are seen in those descended from

him, so, according to the Apostle's declaration, it is necessary that he who was tested in every respect of our life, in our likeness, yet without sin (and the mind is not sin), should share our whole nature. Only so is the apostolic saying true, that we are like him: if it is admitted that he too became like us, so that by becoming such as we are he might make us such as he is. Let us recall once more what he said: "Just as Paul also calls the first Adam a soul, existing with a body and not without a body, but giving the name to the whole, although it is also called soul [?] on its own, by including the spirit." Whoever says this admits that three things are called by the name "soul" by inclusion, as though the meanings of both body and spirit were contained in the same term. "But the last one," he says, "Paul calls a life-giving spirit." In Adam's case he showed that the name prevailed over the other things it signified because of what predominated. The same principle must surely have equal force in this case too. If Adam is called a soul because he sinned, then the man blended with God is named spirit as a whole, because "he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth." But he will not accept this sense. He says that the former is earthy, from the earth, because the body formed from dust was given a soul. Was the mind, then, which he calls spirit, not put in along with the forming of Adam? In what, then, did Adam's likeness to God consist? And what was the outflow from the divine breath, if these are not believed to be the mind? He says that the latter is called "from heaven" for this reason: because the heavenly Spirit became flesh. What Scripture says this? To which of the saints does he attribute the statement that the Spirit became flesh? That is not what we have heard from the Gospels. That is not what we were taught by the Apostle's great voice. The proclamation says that the Word became flesh, and the gospel narrative says that the Spirit descended in the form of a dove. But none of those who received mysteries through the Spirit ever spoke of the Spirit becoming flesh. "Glory dwelt in our land," and "Truth sprang up from the earth," and "God was revealed in the flesh," and "Righteousness looked down from heaven," and many other such sayings. But divinely inspired Scripture knows nothing of a Spirit becoming flesh. "And the man Christ pre-exists," he says, "not as though the Spirit, that is, God, were other than he, but in that the Lord, in the nature of the God-man, is divine Spirit." These

are the writer's words verbatim. Because of the feebleness of his powers of expression, his meaning is not very clear. So I will first strip the underlying sense out of the murk of his wording, and then add the [?] examination. "The man Christ pre-exists," he says. He thinks of the man who appeared together with the Word who was in the beginning, as though that man had existed before he was manifested, and he develops the notion in what follows. He says that the Spirit is not other than him, and by this he argues that the very Godhead of the Son was a man from the beginning. This is shown more clearly by the next statement: "the Lord, in the nature of the God-man, being divine Spirit." He has made one nature of God and man, and called the fusion of the two [spirits] by one name. This, then, is the sense of his words: what was revealed in the flesh born of the Virgin is to be thought of as existing before all things, not only in the eternity of the Godhead, as we all believe, but in the flesh itself too. In support of this view he adds "Before Abraham came to be, I am," and John's saying "He was before me," and "One Lord, through whom are all things," and "He is before all things," and a certain saying of Zechariah, which we will pass over, since it has been dragged forcibly to serve this purpose. If his construction of absurdity were hidden under some cloak of ideas, I would rightly take pains to expose what lay concealed. But since it shouts its impiety openly, I do not know what more my words could accomplish. If the flesh existed before the ages, if what came from Mary existed before Abraham came to be, then the Virgin is older than Nahor, and Mary existed before Adam. But why do I say this? She is apparently older than the very formation of the world, and more ancient than the ages themselves. For if he became flesh in the Virgin, and the flesh is called Jesus, and the Apostle testifies that he is before all things, then apparently our fine fellow makes Mary too coeternal with the Father. And I say nothing of the far more unseemly consequences that the absurdity of his empty novelty leads to. A sharp-witted person would see the absurdity from what follows, even if we do not spell out its indecency in words.

But let us pass by the stench of these notions, noting only this much. If the flesh existed before the ages, then the Godhead has not emptied itself. The Son was not in the form of God and did not put on the form of a servant. What he was by nature was simply revealed now, and he was not humbled. May the Word be gracious to my words, but I keep silent about the rest. If the flesh exists before all things, then all things come from weakness, not from power: "For the spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak." Does he even stop his absurdity there? Who would not see from what follows the things bound up with this? He will surely have to think of all the properties of the flesh as belonging to the one who existed with flesh before the ages: weariness, grief, tears, thirst, sleep, the want caused by hunger, and what is still more absurd than that. Then there is the fact that "a child has been born to us," as the divine voice says, and that the Lord was seen by the shepherds in swaddling clothes. Luke too says that "Jesus advanced in stature and wisdom and grace," being made complete as he grew to the full measure of manhood, walking the road of nature. What will those who see the flesh as existing before the ages say to all this? What size of body did he have before the ages? For he passed through every age of human life. Was that man who exists before all creation a child, or a newborn infant, or a youth, or a full-grown body from the start? If they say a child, they will surely also have to explain why, after so long an age had passed, he had not yet reached full stature. If they say full-grown, we shall ask them to explain how, in his human birth, he was shrunk down to the smallness of an infant. Where did he leave the surplus of his body? How was its bulk reduced to so small a compass? And then again, how did he restore his body to its own size? By recovering, through gradual growth, what he had from the beginning, or by adding new matter to himself through food? If they say it was the original body, they will show that food was entirely superfluous. But if they do not deny that the Lord ate food, what will they say about the flesh left behind above? Presumably most of it was left behind, and only as much was taken from it as the Virgin's womb could hold. No doubt they will tell some marvel about this too, and build further doctrines on it, wherever the logic of their absurd fables necessarily drives them.

But let this too be passed over. One might, not unreasonably, ask the following of those who teach that the divine incarnation existed before the ages. If they think that the flesh was always about him, they are saying that the flesh is God. But all flesh resists the touch. What resists the touch is material and composite, and what is composite can also be dissolved. It is therefore entirely unavoidable that on these terms he too is made out to be material, composed of different elements, and by nature awaiting dissolution. For we know what his body was composed of when he lived among human beings as a man. It too consisted of flesh and bones and blood, like everyone else's. We know this from the marks of the nails, from the blood poured out at the thrust of the spear, and from what the Lord said to those who did not believe what they saw: "Touch me and see, and know that a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have." If, then, the divine incarnation did not have its beginning from the Virgin, as Apolinarius says, but existed before Abraham and before all creation, it was surely such as the disciples saw: solid, resisting the touch, and made up of flesh and bones. These things, then, always existed, and he never descended to lowliness at all. What was hidden, being divine by nature, was simply revealed at the time of the incarnation. What did Arius, or Eunomius, who is worse than he, ever devise to destroy the glory of the Only-begotten that compares with what Apolinarius constructs for us in such a treatise? A God in flesh before the ages, bony, made up of skin and sinews and flesh and fat, composed of different parts, without simplicity and freedom from composition in himself! But the Word who was in the beginning, and was with God, and was both Word and God, in the last days became flesh out of love for humankind, through fellowship with the lowliness of our nature. For this reason he was blended with man and received our whole nature into himself, so that by being blended with the Divine the human might be deified together with it, and the whole lump of our nature sanctified together through that firstfruits. [?] …

[?] … to [?] the argument. As evidence that he always existed in flesh and blood, he cited the apostolic saying that through him we have received redemption, through his blood the forgiveness of sins, through his flesh. I do not think anyone with any sense would doubt that this points to a different meaning. Who does not know the divine mystery, that the author of our salvation goes in search of the lost sheep? We human beings are that sheep, who strayed away through sin from the rational hundred. And he takes the whole sheep on his own shoulders. The sheep had not strayed only in part. Since the whole of it had wandered off, the whole of it is brought back. The hide is not carried home while the innards are left behind, as Apolinarius would have it. Once on the shepherd's shoulders, that is, in the Lord's Godhead, the sheep becomes one with him by being taken up. That is why, wishing to seek and to save the lost, he took up on himself what he had found when he found what he sought. The sheep did not move on its own feet, which had once gone astray, but was carried by the Godhead. Therefore what appeared was a sheep, that is, a man. "But his footprints were not known," as it is written. For he who carried the sheep on himself left no footprint of sin or straying on the human nature. What appeared were the kind of footprints it was fitting for God to leave along the path of life: teachings, healings, the raising of the dead, and the other miracles. Having taken this sheep on himself, the shepherd became one with it. That is why he speaks to the flock with the sheep's voice. How could human weakness have endured the impact of a divine voice? Instead he speaks to us humanly, or, as one might say, sheep-wise, saying, "My sheep hear my voice." So the shepherd who took the sheep up on himself and speaks to us through it is both sheep and shepherd: a sheep in what was taken up, a shepherd in the one who took it up. The good shepherd had to lay down his life for the sheep, so that by his own death he might destroy death. So the author of our salvation then becomes both, in his human nature: both priest and lamb, carrying out his death in that which was able to share in suffering. Death is nothing other than the separation of soul and body. Having united himself to both, I mean to the soul and to the body, he is separated from neither. [?] Irrevocable … [?]

[?] …for the gifts of God [are irrevocable], as the Apostle says. Rather, having divided himself between the body and the soul, through the soul he opens paradise to the thief, and through the body he halts the working of corruption. And this is the destruction of death: that corruption is made powerless, abolished in the life-giving nature. For what happened in these becomes a benefit and grace common to our whole nature. And so he who is in both joins together, through the resurrection, everything that had been separated. By his own authority he gave the body to the heart of the earth, as it is written, and laid down the soul from himself, saying to the Father, "Into your hands I commit my spirit," and to the thief, "in paradise." In both sayings he spoke the truth. For we must not believe that divine dwelling, if it is indeed called Paradise, to be anywhere else than in the spacious palm of the Father, as the prophet also says, addressing the Jerusalem above in the person of the Lord: "On my hands I have painted your walls, and you are before me continually." So, then, he both comes to be in death and is not mastered by death. For what is composite is divided, but what is incomposite admits no dissolution. The incomposite nature remains when the composite is divided, and when the soul departs from the body, it is separated from neither. The proof is its working, as has been said: in the body it produced incorruption, and in the soul the dwelling in paradise. The simple and incomposite one is not split apart along with the separation of these. On the contrary, he brings about oneness, for by being undivided in himself he also brings what was divided into union. He shows this in saying that "God raised him from the dead." For in the case of the Lord's resurrection it is not pious to suppose that, like Lazarus or any other of those brought back to life, he is restored to life by a power not his own. Rather, the Only-begotten God himself raises up the man who was blended with him. He both separated the soul from the body and united the two again, and in this way the common salvation of our nature comes about. Hence he is also called the Author of life. For in him who died and was raised for us, the Only-begotten God reconciled the world to himself, [ransoming] us like captives taken by the spear, through the blood that is akin to ours…

[?] …the more pious [view?], whether, as we say, the glory by dispensation dwells in our land, or, as he says, the flesh does not become an acquired addition to the Godhead for the sake of the benefaction but is co-essential and connatural with it. If the prophet Zechariah is applied in his riddles to one of these, I think there is no need to examine in this discussion whether the meaning looks to the Lord or to someone else. For he says: "Sword, awake against my shepherd, and against the man who is my kinsman." We think the passage moves the sword threateningly against those who have dealt unjustly with their own kin. Apolinarius, however, says that the sword is raised against the Lord because of the title "shepherd." He does not know that in many places Scripture calls those appointed to rule both shepherds and herdsmen. Again, whatever he drags in from the Epistle to the Hebrews for the same purpose shows such obvious absurdity in its arguments that anyone with even a little sense can easily see it. For since it is written that "In these last days God, who formerly spoke to the fathers in the prophets in many parts and in many ways, has spoken to us in a Son," this, he says, is proof that the humanity of the God who appeared to us is before the ages. These are his exact words, offered supposedly as an interpretation of the Apostle: "It is clear from these words that the very man who spoke to us the things of the Father is God, the maker of the ages, the radiance of glory, the imprint of his substance, since he is God by his own spirit and does not have within himself another God besides himself. He himself, through himself, that is, through the flesh, cleansed the world of sins." This is what Apolinarius says, word for word, and we have altered nothing in what he said. If, then, the man who spoke is the maker of the ages, as the writer thinks, and the flesh is the radiance, and the form of the slave expresses the substance of God, it no longer seems right to me to fight against what he has said. Rather, I should lament the insensibility of those who accept such novel talk. A man spoke to us in human fashion with our voice, spat with his mouth and made clay with his hand, put his fingers into the ears of the deaf, and touched the sick and the dead. He rested from weariness by sleeping and sitting, wept, was distressed and grieved, felt hunger, took food, and asked for water. Is this one, in his very fleshly and human being, conceived as existing before the constitution of the world? And is the composite nature of flesh, solid and resistant to the touch, called God? Let the hearing of all the pious be stopped. [Notes: (17) Correction: τοῦτον ("this one"). (18) Correction: ῥᾴδιον εἶναι καί ("to be easy, and"). (19) [?] ὁ ἄνθρωπος ("the man").]

…and may the divine and pure doctrines not be defiled by being outraged with fleshlier passions by those who insult the Divine. For who does not know that the God who was manifested to us in the flesh is, according to the teaching of the pious tradition, immaterial, invisible and incomposite? He was and is unbounded and uncircumscribed, being everywhere and pervading the whole of creation. Yet in what appeared he was seen within a human circumscription. For every body must necessarily be contained by some surface. This surface, then, is the boundary of the body enclosed within it. Everything contained by a boundary is enclosed within some definite quantity, and what is bounded cannot be unbounded. Yet the Prophet says, "Of his greatness there is no end." If, then, the divine nature, as the wri[ter]… [Notes: (23) Correction: ἐξανθρωπιζόντων ("who make the Divine human"). (24) Correction: τῇ σαρκί ("in the flesh"). (25) Correction: ἀόριστός τε καί ("both unbounded and"). (27) Correction: [?] ὅρῳ περιεχόμενον ("contained by a boundary"). [?] …the one who spoke to us the things of the [Father?] [?] …thoughts and names [?].]

[?] …that the incorporeal is given its imprint by a body, and the visible shines forth from the invisible. But the radiance is plainly of the same kind as the glory, and the substance is surely of the same kind as the imprint. So if the one is a body, we cannot suppose that the other is incorporeal either. He also mentions the doctrine of Nicaea, at which the common synod of the Fathers proclaimed the term "consubstantial." No one would call something of a different kind consubstantial. The term "consubstantial" fits only things that share one and the same definition of essence. Suppose, then, that the Son is a fleshly God, being by nature flesh in the very thing he is, according to the pre-eternal name. Suppose too, as the writer himself does not dispute, that he is consubstantial with the Father. Things are consubstantial with each other when they are described by the same definition of essence. It follows that Apolinarius makes the nature of the Father something human and fleshly as well, so as to keep the name "consubstantial" for both. For he must take one of two options. If he calls the Father incorporeal and the Godhead of the Son fleshly, he will be agreeing that they are of different essences. If he confesses that Father and Son share Godhead and essence alike, he will make the nature of the Godhead fleshly in the Father too. As if to correct this absurdity, he says in an earlier passage, interpreting Zechariah's saying as he sees fit, that "kinsman" was spoken in the person of the Father about the Son, and means connatural and consubstantial. Whether he understood this correctly or not is another question. In any case, this is what he argues: "The prophetic word shows by these things," he says, "that he is consubstantial with God not according to the flesh but according to the spirit that is united to the flesh." How, then, is his fleshly God united to flesh before the world was constituted? For when the ages did not yet exist, neither did anything else in creation. And flesh is the least and last of the things that came to be in creation. What flesh, then, was he united to, when human nature had not yet come into being? Perhaps he knows of some other flesh besides that of man. Then how does he say that "the very man who spoke to us the things of the Father is God, the maker of the ages"? Who will explain to us the absurdity of these novel riddles? A man before man came to be, flesh existing before its own creation, and something that came to be in the last times being pre-eternal… [Notes: (34) The text reads: χαρακτηρίζεσθαι μὲν σώματι τὸ ἀόρατον ἀπαυγάζεσθαι ("that the invisible is imprinted by a body, shines forth"). (36) [?] …"the writer does not dispute that it is." (38) Correction: διὰ τοῦ Υἱοῦ ("through the Son").]

…and whatever other such things he goes through in a confused way in his treatise. But let the writer wander as he pleases in the trackless wastes of his reasonings. We will set out the apostolic teaching that he himself cited, as a refutation of these impious notions, and then press on to what follows in the argument. "Who, being in the form of God," it says. It did not say "having a form like God," which is said of what was made after the likeness of God. It said "being in the very form of God," for all that belongs to the Father is in the Son. Therefore eternity, freedom from quantity, immateriality and incorporeality are in the Son as well, so that the form of the Father's imprint may be preserved in the Son in every respect. "And being equal to God": what idea of difference or variation does equality leave room for? How could "equal" be applied to things that differ in nature? For if one is fleshly in nature and the other is pure of flesh, how could anyone make such a being equal to one who is not such [?]? "He emptied himself," it says, "taking the form of a slave." What is the form of a slave? Surely the body, for we have heard of nothing else besides this from the Fathers. So the one who said that he took the form of a slave, and the form is flesh, is saying that he, being one thing in the divine form, took the form of a slave, which by nature is something else. The word "emptied" also shows clearly that he was not always what appeared to us. He was in the fullness of the Godhead equal to God, unapproachable and inaccessible, and above all beyond the capacity of our insignificant human smallness to contain. He became containable by the perishable nature of the flesh at the time when he emptied, as the Apostle says, the ineffable glory of his Godhead and contracted it to our smallness. So what he was remained great, perfect and incomprehensible, while what he took was equal in size to the measure of our nature. "For being made in the likeness of man," it says, "and in fashion": clearly as one who did not have the likeness of such a nature about him from the beginning, nor was shaped after any bodily pattern. For how could the pattern of a shape be imprinted around the incorporeal? He comes to be in fashion at the moment when, taking on a shape, he puts it around himself. And this is the nature of the body… [Note: (40) Correction: ἀχώρητον ("uncontainable").]

[?] …[by the] activity directed toward the construction of his own creature, he is found to be not a common man in every respect, because of the difference in his constitution, but "as a man." And so "he humbled himself," becoming man without change. For if he had been this from the beginning, in what would his humbling have consisted? As it is, the Most High humbled himself through union with the lowliness of our nature. For having been united to the form of the slave that he took, and having become one with it, he makes the sufferings of the slave his own. Something similar happens in us through the natural connection of our limbs. If something befalls the tip of a fingernail, the whole body is affected together with the part that suffered, because the shared sensation pervades the whole body. In the same way, the one who was united to our nature makes our sufferings his own, as Isaiah says: "He took up our infirmities and bore our diseases." He underwent the blow on our behalf, so that by his bruise we might be healed. It was not the Godhead that was bruised, but the man joined to the Godhead through the union, whose nature is capable of receiving a bruise. These things happen so that the road of evil might be undone by retracing the same roads. For since death entered through the disobedience of the man, it is driven out through the obedience of the second man. This is why he becomes obedient unto death: so that through obedience he might heal the transgression that came from disobedience, and through the resurrection from the dead abolish the death that entered along with disobedience. For the resurrection of the man from death is the abolition of death. "Therefore," it says, "God also highly exalted him." This is like a seal on the preceding thought. For it is clear that the Most High needs no exalting. It is the lowly that is raised to the height, now becoming what it was not before. The human nature, united to the Lord, is lifted up together with the Godhead. What is exalted is what is raised up from lowliness, and the lowly thing is the form of the slave, which through the exaltation becomes Christ and Lord. The man in Christ was called by a proper name, in the human manner, through the mystery revealed to the Virgin by Gabriel, and so the human, as has been said, was named Jesus. The divine nature, however, cannot be grasped by a name, and the two became one through the blending. For this reason God too is named from the human. For at the name of Jesus every knee shall bow, and the man comes to be above every name. This belongs properly to the Godhead, which cannot be made subject to any [signification] by name… [Notes: (43) Correction: ἀνακράσεως ("blending"). (45) Correction: τοῦ ὑπ' ἀνθρώπου [?]. Perhaps read τοῦ πρώτου ἀνθρώπου ("of the first man").]

…signification, so that, just as the high comes to be in the lowly, the lowly may in turn receive the properties of the high. For as the Godhead is named through the man, so what was lifted up from lowliness together with the Godhead comes to be above every name. And just as the dishonor of the slave's form is referred to the God who was blended with the slave, so too the worship of the Godhead, offered by all creation, is given to what is united to the Godhead. And so at the name of Jesus Christ every knee bends, of things in heaven, on earth and under the earth, and every tongue shall confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, [Latin intrusion in the text: "and in this manner in"] to the glory of God the Father. Amen.
But it seems that he blushes at himself, as it were, and is ashamed of the absurdity of what he has said. In a way he retracts what he had argued and wants to establish that the Son's likeness to men was a later addition. For he says: "Behold, the same Jesus Christ's equality with the Father pre-existing, his likeness to men supervening." He seems to repent of what he said. Let him do so, as long as he turns from his absurd opinion from the heart, and we will stop our refutations. But by what he does, he seems to be laying the foundations of another absurdity in place of the good sense these words show. These are his exact words: "And what could be clearer than these words to show that there is not one with another, perfect God with perfect man?" Anyone who knows how to follow an argument can see that this statement has no connection at all with what came before. For how does a pre-existing equality with the Father and a supervening likeness to men, as he puts it, prove that there was no perfect man through whom the perfect God became man? It is as if someone said that heaven stands apart from the earth, and then claimed that this makes it evident that lead is heavier than tin, treating weight as if it were heavenly distance. In the same way, no one could say that a deficiency in the humanity through which God comes to be in our nature is proved by confessing that the Son's likeness to men was a later addition. I will put off for a little while exposing the impiety and folly of such a notion. For now I will try to go through what he wrote, in order and word for word, [taking up] whatever is open to blame at first glance [?]. He says that there is not perfect God with perfect man. Here, for the moment, he has left it ambiguous which of the two he named [as imperfect], and by the…

…obscurity of what he means, his thought looks in both directions [?]. From what we have heard, there is no way to tell about which of the two the imperfection is taught: about God, or about the man, or whether he thinks it applies equally to both. He says that he is God in spirit, having the glory of God, and man in body, having worn the inglorious form of men. He said "God," and he also said "man." It is evident to everyone that these names do not mean the same thing. The account that explains Godhead is one thing, and the account that explains humanity is another. For God is that which is always the same, the cause of all good things, which never was not and never will not be. Man, on the other hand, is in other respects akin to the nature of the irrational animals and, like them, is governed through flesh and sense. But he is set apart from the irrational animals by the addition of mind, and in this lies the distinctive feature of his nature. For no one would define man by flesh, bones and sense organs, and no one who mentioned the powers of nourishment and growth would thereby indicate what is proper to human nature. It is the intellectual and rational that shows what man is. It comes to the same thing, then, to explain a nature by its name or by what properly belongs to that nature. For whoever says "man" indicates the rational, and whoever names the rational has shown man by that word. So when Apolinarius names God and man, if he includes [?] in the one word all the meanings that belong to the Godhead, he would not mutilate the meaning of "man" in his explanation either. But if he is called man, the name is wholly true and not falsely applied, and the truth of the name is shown in the fact that the one so named is a rational animal. Reason surely comes from intellect. So if he is a man, he necessarily has intellect. But if he does not have intellect, neither [is he a man]…

"But he was man in body," he says, "having worn the inglorious form of men." He puts these things forward on his own authority, not from the teaching of Scripture. Still, let us consider the statement in such a way that, from his very own words, what he is striving for may be turned to the opposite. He wore, he says, the inglorious form of men. Let us first examine what the glory of man is, and from that we will understand what ingloriousness is. The glory of man, at least true glory, is surely the life of virtue. For to define the glory or ingloriousness of men by a fine complexion or a youthful bloom of the flesh, or conversely by ugliness of body, would be the view of the effete [?]… [Notes: (58) [?] Perhaps read νομίζει ("thinks"). (64) Correction: διανοητικόν τε καί ("both intellectual and"). (65) Correction: ἐπέδειξεν ("showed"). (66) Correction: εἴπερ πάσας τάς ("if indeed all the").]

…[if] virtue is acknowledged to be what is glorious among men, vice is surely what is inglorious. Yet Apolinarius says that God took on the inglorious form of men. If, then, ingloriousness lies in vice, and vice is a disgrace of the will, and it is the intellect that chooses, and intellect is a movement of the mind, then in seeing human ingloriousness in God he does not cut off from intellect the man through whom God took part in human life. And this agrees with the divine Scriptures, which say that he became sin for us, that is, that he united to himself the sinful soul of man. "The Lord," he says, "appearing in the guise of a slave." Was this slave, whose guise the Lord put on, whole, or was he mutilated? For whatever is deficient and cut short in the completeness of a living being could reasonably be called mutilated. "Not man," he says, "but as man, because he was not consubstantial with man in the most sovereign part." If not consubstantial, then surely of a different essence. And things whose definitions of essence differ share neither a common nature nor a common name. Fire has one essence and water another, and the names of the two differ. But Peter and Paul, since their nature is one, also share the name of their essence, for each of them is a man. Suppose, then, that he was something else in essence and not a man, that he was shaped like a man only as far as appearances went, while in truth he differed in nature. Then let him say that everything was a kind of seeming and a deceptive apparition. On his view the eating was false and the sleep was false. All the miracles of healing were unreal. The cross did not happen, nor the laying in the tomb, nor the resurrection after the passion. Everything appeared only in seeming, and according to the writer's account none of what appeared was real. For if he was not a man, how could the things recorded about him have been real? And how could anyone call someone who is alien to human essence a man? For he was not, he says, consubstantial with man in the most sovereign part. But whoever removes from man his most sovereign part, that is, the mind, has shown that what remains is a beast, and a beast is not a man. Then he says: "Humbled in the flesh, but highly exalted by God with the divine exaltation." This in turn is even more senseless than what came before, as well as impious. He says that one was humbled and another exalted. The flesh, he says, was humbled, although nothing of the…

[Notes: (68) Correction: ὡμολόγηται ("has been acknowledged"). (69) Correction: ἐστὶ τό ("is the"). (70) Correction: ἐστί τι κίνημα ("is a movement"). Perhaps read: ἀλλὰ μὲν μέχρι τοῦ φαιν[ομένου] ("but only as far as appearance") [?].]

Again, like people who babble in their sleep, he drops the logical thread of his argument and borrows our own words. Whatever someone of sound mind might say about the doctrine, he too mixes into his own words. He distinguishes what is glorified from the one who has the glory: "He is glorified," he says, "as man; but he has glory before the world, as God who existed before the ages." Up to this point he is reasonable. If what he says had stopped there, perhaps someone would have thought that he had repented and come round to the more pious view. As it is, he takes this sound idea as a turning-post, rounds it, and runs straight back onto the racecourse of error. He heaps many insults on us and puts our position on a level with that of Jews and Greeks. Then he once more brings up the vomit he had already spewed out in his earlier passages. With his empty words he moulds onto Christ that flesh from before the ages. He says that the Son, being enfleshed mind, was born of a woman. He did not become flesh in the Virgin, but merely passed through her on his way. Such as he was before the ages, he was then made manifest, and the very thing that appeared was fleshly God, or, as he himself calls it, "enfleshed mind." That is why, he says, the crucified one is called "Lord of glory," and why prophecy names him "Lord of hosts." It is also why he speaks with those words of authority and sovereignty: "I say to you," and "I command you," and "I am working," and everything else of the loftier kind. What then will this fine fellow do? Where will he put the breast and the swaddling clothes? The life that takes in nourishment and gives it out, the gradual growth of the body, the sleep, the weariness, the obedience to parents? The distress, the grief, the longing for the Passover, the request for water, the eating of food? The bonds, the slaps, the blows of the scourges, the crown of thorns on the head, the scarlet robe, the mockery with the reed? The spear, the vinegar, the nails, the gall, the linen shroud, the burial, the tomb, the stone? How will he attach these to God? For if his enfleshed God, the one seen through Mary, always was this, and if what appeared was Godhead, then it is the Godhead that suffers all these things. The Godhead is suckled, swaddled and fed. It grows weary, grows up, is filled and is emptied. It sleeps, grieves, is distressed and groans. It feels thirst

and hunger. It runs to the fig tree, not knowing the tree's season for bearing fruit. It does not know the day and the hour. It is beaten, bound and slapped. It has nails driven through it, bleeds, dies, is buried and is laid in a new tomb. Does he then agree that these things are proper and natural to the Godhead that exists before the ages? Does he agree that it would not have been nourished unless it had been suckled, and could not have stayed alive at all unless it had made up its spent strength by eating? And how is his enfleshed God ignorant of that day and hour? How does he not know the season for figs, and that at Passover no fruit fit to eat would be found on the tree? Let him say who it is that is ignorant! Who is it that grieves? Who is it that is hemmed in by perplexity? Who is it that cried out that he had been forsaken by God? If the Godhead of the Father and the Son is one, by whom is he forsaken, as he cried aloud on the cross? Suppose the Godhead is what suffers. The pious agree that the Son shares one Godhead with the Father. Yet the sufferer says, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" How, then, is the Godhead, which is one essence, divided in the suffering? How can one forsake and the other be forsaken, one enter death and the other remain in life, one be put to death and the other raise up what was put to death? He has two choices. He may refuse to confess one Godhead of Father and Son, and then he will show himself to be an advocate of Arius. Or, fighting against Arius, he may say that it is one, and then he will contradict himself and be unable to sustain the fable he has invented. Of necessity, then, he will assign these passible and lowlier sayings and conditions to the human element. He will agree that the nature of God remained unchanging and impassible even while sharing in human sufferings. His own words witness to this, for he said of him: "He is glorified as man, rising up from a state without glory; but he has the glory as God, who existed before the world." That state without glory is surely the passible nature of the flesh. The glory, then, is the eternal power, impassible and pure.

as the Lord says somewhere. But he wants the very flesh that was born to be Godhead, and he wants to establish that God did not appear in flesh. So he says that God, being already enfleshed before the ages, was afterwards born through a woman, and came to experience sufferings in accordance with the necessity of nature. In saying this he does not even allow him to be a man. He subjects him to the passions as a man, but gives him no share in human nature. For how can something that is said not to be from the earth be a man? Scripture says that humankind came from Adam, and that Adam first sprang from the earth through divine power. That is why Luke, tracing the genealogy of the one who was supposed to be the son of Joseph, ends with "son of Adam," attaching the beginning of descent to each of the fathers in turn. So one who did not come from the human race is surely something else, and not a man. He is not a man, since he has nothing of the human race. He is not God, since he is not incorporeal. What, then, is this enfleshed God of our speechwriter? Let the disciples and advocates of his deception tell us! "But," he says, "Greeks and Jews would have accepted it if we said that the one born was a man inspired by God, like Elijah." Yet which of the Greeks ever accepted the miracles of Elijah as true? They would have to believe that fire took a double shape, one part in the form of a chariot and the other in the shape of horses, and moved against its own nature, travelling from above downwards. They would have to believe that Elijah, raised aloft on the flaming chariot and driving the fire, was kept unharmed in the flame, while fire drew fire: the fire in the horses drawing the fire in the chariot. If someone accepts these things in the proper way, these very accounts will lead him to accept the mystery. He will see in the narrative a figurative prophecy of the Lord's becoming man, foreshadowed in what took place. Fire by nature rises upward, yet by divine power it came down to earth. Elijah, enveloped in the heavenly fire, was lifted up with it as it returned to its natural motion. In the same way, a certain essence without matter or form, the power of the Most High, took up the form of a slave, which had come into being through the Virgin. It raised that form to its own height and transformed it into the divine and pure nature. So the person who is reluctant to believe this would not assent to Elijah's wonder-working either. And the person who has first learned the truth sketched in shadow there would not oppose the truth itself. Then he turns his abuse on us, who do not accept the fable he has invented, and

says: "But those who are faithless under the guise of faith are ashamed, as the Jews were, of the God who was born of a woman and crucified by the Jews (and that is why he too will be ashamed of them)." Who does not know that hurling curses at opponents is typical of people who are weak in the cause they are pursuing? But we say this much. Two chasms lie before us: on one side the fall of Apollinarius, on the other the fall of Arius. Those who fall into either one are equally shattered. Yet if one must choose between evils, the fracture of Arius seems the lighter. Both drag the pure nature of the Only-begotten down to something lower. Arius makes the Master of the angels akin to the incorporeal nature of the angels, declaring that he and they alike fall short of the uncreated nature and owe their existence to creation. But this man pushes the absurdity so far that he ranks him equal in honour even with man, who is made lower than the angels, and declares his nature to be fleshly. Incorporeal nature is better than bodies, and by the same margin the impiety of Arius is preferable to the error of Apollinarius. Who, then, is faithless under the guise of faith in interpreting the mystery of the Virgin? I will set before everyone both our faith, which the speechwriter mocks, and his own opinion. We say that God, who is without matter, form or body in his essence, by a certain loving dispensation, toward the end of the completion of the universe, when evil had already

having made [?]. He says that he grew weary when he went from Judea to Galilee. He says that for the Israelites he turned the rock into pools of water, yet himself asked a Samaritan woman for a drink. He says that for forty years he poured out heavenly food on so many tens of thousands without tiring, yet himself ran to the fig tree hoping for food that was not there. Such is the understanding of the doctrine on each side. Let the intelligent hearer judge for himself who is faithless under the guise of faith. But he says that we claim the crucified one had nothing divine in his own nature, not even the most sovereign element, that is, spirit. Against such a slander a defence lies ready to hand: we simply deny it. If Apollinarius takes "spirit" to mean mind, no Christian says that the man blended with God was half a man. Rather, the whole man was united to the divine power. One may call the parts of a man by whatever names one likes: mind, spirit or heart. Scripture uses all three for the ruling faculty: "Create in me a clean heart, O God"; and "The one with understanding will gain guidance"; and "No one knows the things of a man except the spirit that is in him." Through the overshadowing of the power of the Most High and the coming of the Holy Spirit, he was not without spirit, nor without mind, nor without heart. So the abuse is not aimed at us, as though we said that that man came into being without the spirit, that is, the mind, in himself. It is aimed at the very author of the abuse, who pelts us with his own reproaches. He calls the mind "spirit," and he says that the man in Christ had no mind. So it is he who makes out that the Lord had no spirit. But what is the next charge? He says that we do wrong when we claim that the man had something greater beyond his own nature, namely the Godhead dwelling in him. If he counts this as a charge, we do not run from the accusation, since we are thrown out together with the Apostle. We learned this from him, and we believe that, being in the form of God as regards what is perceived by the mind, he comes to be in the form of a slave as regards what appears. If the divine form is more honourable than the person of the slave, then what appears is certainly not equal in honour to what is hidden. So what was seen in the flesh and lived among men had within it something more honourable than itself. Yet the speechwriter turns this into a charge against the faith. But the Apostle also says that in him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily. In saying "in him," he did not mean half of what is referred to, but included the whole subject in the meaning. So if the Godhead dwelt in a human body, and that body was not without a soul, and the rational part is proper to the human soul

... For if this were separated, then, as we have often said, what is left is a beast. So then this fine fellow is attacking with his abuse not us, but the Apostle, and more than that, the great saying of John: "The Word became flesh and dwelt among us." John did not mean a part of us. With the plural word he included everything that is understood to belong to our nature. He first distinguished the Word from the flesh, and only then brought them into union. For the Word existed by himself and was with God; and what God was, the Word also was, for he too was God. But when he came to his own and shone in the darkness, then the Word became flesh, becoming flesh in the Virgin by his own power. So let him spare us his abuse, lest he include the saints in it through the [?]. Passing over the intervening material, in which he supposes that those who do not share his views deny the truths of the mystery, I will mention one of the things he said in his tirade to slander us. He says that unless we say what he says, we can say neither that he existed before his birth on earth, nor that he is before all things, nor that he is of the same race as God. Now we do confess that he existed before his earthly birth, since we do not doubt that the flesh is of earthly make-up [?]. But as for "of the same race as God," away with it! Let no Christian coin words so lowly and so foreign to the divine majesty as to proclaim the one who truly is God "of the same race as God," rather than true God. Not even Eunomius would hold back from such an expression about the Lord. For he too, though he does not accept that his Godhead is true, might say that he is of the same race as God. He would mean it in the sense that those who have accepted faith in him become of one body with Christ and sharers with him: they are not what the Lord is, but they partake of him and share the name of what they partake of. So the man who accuses us of not saying these things, which the pious do not confess, has borne witness that our doctrine is pious and beyond reproach. Then, to establish that the flesh is Godhead,

the one who leapt in his mother's womb, who received with exultation the sound of the greeting of the Lord's mother, would also himself be holy from birth. The angel's words about him declare as much: "And he will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother's womb." But he adds this to what he has said: "Who is wise without being taught?" We say that the Wisdom of God, which is Christ, is not taught but teaches. But we have no doubt that the portion of our flesh united to the divine Wisdom received the gift of wisdom by participation. We trust the Gospel, which says: "And Jesus increased in stature and in wisdom and in grace." In the body, gradual growth advances toward full development of nature with the help of food. In the same way, in the soul, progress toward perfect wisdom comes through training to those who pursue it. "Who," he asks, "does the works of God with authority?" How he belittles the ineffable majesty of the Lord with childish arguments! Doing the works of God with authority belongs also to men who have been granted divine power. Elijah was such a man. By his authority he released the rain for people and shut it off. He brought down fire on his opponents. He made flour grow in the jar and oil gush forth in the flask. By breathing on a lifeless body he gave it life, and he did all the other things the record tells of him. So it is nothing beyond a man to work some miracle by God's authority and divine power. What is beyond a man is to be oneself the supreme power. This is what we, and all who have received the word in truth, believe. But the division he has thoughtlessly added to these remarks we will leave to the reflections of the learned, since it is not fitting for us to refute it seriously. What does he mean by "dividing the activity according to the flesh, but making it equal according to the spirit"? He tacked this onto the Gospel saying, "My Father is working until now, and I am working." If anyone is able to plead for the senseless, let him stand up for the argument. Let him tell us what the author means when he adds the same kind of thing again, in these exact words: "Which again has equality in power and the division of activity according to the flesh, by which," he says, "he did not give life to all, but to some, whom he willed." For our part, we take the simple and unadorned sense of divine Scripture, and so we understand these words as follows.

We hear the Lord explaining that "the Father raises the dead and gives them life, and the Son gives life to whom he wills." We do not take this to mean that some are excluded from his life-giving will. We have heard, and we believe, that everything that belongs to the Father belongs to the Son. Clearly, then, we see the Father's will in the Son too, as one of those "all things." So the Father's will is in the Son. And the Father, as the Apostle says, "wills all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth." It follows that he who possesses everything that is the Father's, and has the whole Father in himself, certainly has in himself, along with the Father's other good things, the whole of the saving will. If, then, he does not fall short of the perfect will, it is perfectly clear that he gives life to those whom the Father wills to be given life. He is not inferior in his loving will, as Apollinarius claims when he says that he willed some, not all, to be given life. Some are saved and others perish, but the Lord's will is not the reason; otherwise the blame for those who perish would go back to it. Rather, some are saved and some perish according to the free choice of those who receive the word. He adds to his arguments: "No one died or rose again by his own authority." Having said this, he cites the saying of the Gospel: "No one takes my soul from me; I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again." What kind of soul is this, rational or irrational? I would put that question to those who join a mindless soul to God. If they say irrational, they will be saying that what belonged to Christ was a beast, not a man. If they say rational, what do they suppose thought to be, if not reason? Reason is not a sound without meaning. It is a movement of thought, which becomes the source and basis of speech. So anyone who has said "rational soul" has also admitted that it thinks. And thinking is a movement and activity of the mind. How could the mind act if it were not present, if they declare that the Lord's soul has no share in mind? So the Lord has a soul, which by his own authority he both takes up and lays down. It is not a bestial and irrational soul, but one belonging to the human make-up. It is therefore acknowledged without question that, since he took on a human soul, it is a thinking soul.

After saying these things, he speaks about the grain that dies and then springs up again with more grains. Since that passage is on our side and confirms our argument, I will gladly pass over it. For what is the grain that dies and, in its own ear of resurrection, raises a heap of grains along with itself? I do not think anyone is so uninitiated in the divine doctrines as not to see that the mystery of the passion concerns the man. The proof of this is that we too die with him, are buried with him, and rise with him. For it is easy for those who wish it to imitate what is of their own kind, but to become like what transcends them is impossible. So if it was flesh that underwent death, it would be easier for us also, who live in the flesh, to imitate that death by our death. But if the Godhead died, how shall we who are in the flesh die together with the Godhead? Flesh dies with flesh and rises with it. But if the Godhead suffered this, as Apolinarius would have it, we must look for other godheads that will die and rise together with the Godhead. For "just as Christ died and rose, so shall we also," says the Apostle. What are we by our own nature? Divine power, or blood and flesh, as Scripture says? This is why he who for our sake became like us shared flesh and blood with us for our sake. Therefore he who died for us was what we are in essence, and so the imitation of him is set before those of the same kind. And a proof of the impiety of the argument that declares mortal [?]

[?] for in the common death of men, what is it that dies and decays? Does not the flesh dissolve into earth, while the mind remains with the soul and suffers no harm to its being even when the body is removed? The evidence is that the rich man remembers the things above the earth and pleads with Abraham for those related to him by kinship.
