No one would call it a sign of a mind gone that, knowing his own fate to be inescapable, he took some thought for those close to him. If, then, our mind endures even after death, impassible and unchanged, how is it likely that that God of Apolinarius, the third part, underwent the death of the flesh? How did he die, or in what way did he suffer the dissolution of death? For no one at all is unaware that death is the separation of soul and body from each other. But the soul itself, and the intellect—how is it divided from itself, so that it too might receive death? If, then, our soul cannot receive death, how does it receive death? Let those who chop Christ into portions tell us.

"But they are troubled," he says, "with the trouble of the unbelieving." He hurls this insult at us, calling troubled and unbelieving those who heed without questioning the voice of the Gospel, which says, "If it is possible, let this cup pass from me; yet not my will but yours be done." To this he adds his own words, which run as follows: "And they do not remember," he says, "that this will is said to belong not to the man from the earth, as they themselves suppose, but to God who came down from heaven." What could one find to match such a statement? I do not mean among those condemned for heresy; I do not think even the father of impiety and lies himself could find anything more dreadful in the way of blasphemy than these words. Does the writer know what he is saying? God, having come down from heaven, sets aside the proper will of the Godhead, and does not want what he wants to be carried out! Then the wills of the Son and the Father are divided. And how could the will be common to both? How could identity of nature be shown by difference of wills? For the will must necessarily go together with the nature, as the Lord says somewhere: "A good tree cannot bear bad fruit, nor can a rotten tree bear good fruit." Choice would be the fruit of nature, so that a good nature has a good choice, and an evil nature an evil one. If, then, the fruit of the will differs in the Father and the Son, they are confessing that the nature of each must necessarily differ too. Why then is Arius opposed? Why do they not desert to Eunomius? For he, dividing the nature of the Father and the Son, cuts the will apart along with the nature, and on this especially he builds his case that their essence is foreign, splitting the definition of the Godhead between the inferior and the superior. But let us take up again what he said: "They do not remember," he says, "that this will is said to belong not to the man from the earth, as they suppose, but to God who came down from heaven." Which will does the writer mean? Clearly the one the Lord wishes not to be done, when he says to the Father, "Not my will, but yours be done." Does he understand what contradiction his argument has fallen into? The passion is drawing near, the betrayer is just about to arrive with the crowd, and it is then that this prayer is made. The one

praying: is he man or God? If he thinks the one praying is God, he sees in him the same weakness as in men. How then is he God, if he has no good of his own but needs help from above? And then, how does the Godhead condemn its own will? Was what he wanted good or bad? If good, why is what he wanted not carried through? If bad, what kinship has the Godhead with evil? But, as I said, he does not understand that he is turning his argument into its opposite. For if the voice that says, "Not my will be done, but yours," belongs to the only-begotten God, the argument keeps turning upon itself through a contradiction and never comes to rest. For one who does not want his own will to be done wants precisely this: that what he wants should not be done. How then will the prayer be fulfilled, when he says, "I want this: that what I want should not happen"? It will be turned entirely against what is sought, and whoever hears such a prayer will be at a loss either way. For whatever he does, he turns the outcome to what the one praying does not want. Will he do what the one praying wants? But the prayer is that what he wants should not be done. Will he not do what he wants? But the one praying wants what he does not want to happen to him. So, whichever way it is taken, the idea will mislead, fighting against itself and destroyed by itself. For such perplexity in the argument there could be only one remedy: the true confession of the mystery, that shrinking from the passion belongs to human weakness—as the Lord himself says, when he says that the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak—while enduring the passion appointed by the divine plan belongs to the divine will and power. Since, then, the human will is one thing and the divine another, he who made our sufferings his own speaks, as from the man, words suited to the weakness of the nature; but he adds the second utterance because he wishes the lofty will befitting God to be ratified over the human will, for the sake of mankind's

salvation. For when he said, "Not mine," he signified the human element by that word; and by adding "yours," he showed the union of his own Godhead with the Father, in which there is no difference of will because they share one nature. For in speaking of the Father's will he also indicated the Son's. And this will is that all men should be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth, which could not have come about otherwise unless death, which blocks the way to life, were swallowed up. The Lord makes his own the lowly words and the feeling of human fear, showing that what is ours was truly in him, and confirming the nature by sharing in its sufferings. "But it was not," says Apolinarius, "of the man from the earth, as they suppose, but of God who came down from heaven, that which was assumed into union with him." In these words the feebleness and obscurity of the expression lead the reader of the text away from following the sense; yet the meaning is not entirely hidden by the confusion of the wording. "Not of the man from the earth," he says, "are those words full of suffering, but of God who came down from heaven." Up to this point his intention is clear from what he says: he is trying to establish that the Godhead is subject to suffering. Then he confuses the meaning by the absurdity of his expression. For after saying "of God who came down from heaven," he adds, "what was assumed into union with him"—as if someone were to put the statement more plainly: "It was not a man who spoke, but God spoke through the man, having taken what was seen into union with himself." Where, then, was the man assumed from? From heaven? From earth? Not from earth, he says. But a being that came to be in the heavens is not of human kind. It remains to say that he came from nowhere, and this also implies that what was seen was mere appearance and not reality; for what comes from nowhere does not exist at all. Yet from the words he has set out, he says that the man came down from heaven. And yet Mary was on earth, the cave was in the earth, and the manger was earthly. How, then, does he transplant a man for us from heaven to earth? For while all Scripture confesses the Virgin, the birth, the flesh, the swaddling clothes, the breast, the manger, the human condition, he leaves all this aside and another [?]

[?] doctrine. As for the passages in which he attacks us more violently with blasphemies, I think a person of sense ought to pass them over and leave it to the ears of the readers to judge who are the counterfeiters of the apostolic faith: we, who in Paul's words once knew Christ according to the flesh but now know him so no longer, or he who always, both before the dispensation by which he became man and after it, carries his own fleshly God about in his argument. He adds the blasphemy uttered against him by the Jews, that they called him a glutton and a drunkard, and says that these things necessarily apply to the man. Who, then, is the man the Jews reproached for eating and drinking? Did he partake of these things, or not? If he did not partake, it was mere appearance; if he did, what he partook of was earthly, and what is heavenly is not nourished by earthly things. What contradictory absurdities! How he is thrown down in opposite directions at one and the same time! At one moment he says that the one who appeared in bodily form is superior to human nature; then again he shows him to be inferior even to men, mutilated in his better part. For what is preeminent in us is the intellect, and he says the flesh in which God was manifested had no share in it. He sets this out clearly in the arguments that follow, which we shall run through briefly, unless one thinks it superfluous to examine vain things carefully. For once again, after pouring a flood of insults into his treatise, he advances an argument of this sort against us, saying that those who claim that "union of flesh" and "assumption of man" are the same thing are in the wrong. But I will not hide the truth, even if what I say seems rather rustic: our plain way of speaking does not define either of these expressions precisely. It is not easy to explain offhand how "union of flesh" differs from "assumption of man," because union is understood in many ways: by number, by form, by nature, by pursuits, by learning, and by the properties and pursuits that belong to vice or to virtue. What, then, is the union of the flesh, whether it is united with itself or with something else? We need those who interpret the expression to tell us. And how the assumption of the man takes place—what sort of man is assumed, from where, how, by whom, and in what manner—is just as unknown to us as the former. For until he presents his account of the mystery seasoned with the divine salt of Scripture, let us leave the salt of outside wisdom, which has lost its savor, to be trampled underfoot by the faithful. Which of the evangelists told of a "union of flesh"? Which of the apostolic narratives taught the "assumption of the man"

in so many words? What law, what prophets, what inspired word, what decree of a synod has handed down any such thing to us? Of these two phrases, then, he assigns one to us and says the other is his own; but which of them he claims as his own, we are still unsure even now. For we either make neither of them our own, or both, because we find no difference between the one and the other. Union is always with something, and assumption is always of something; each implies a relation to something else. The one who assumes is united with what is assumed, and what is united has been united by assumption. But he says that we speak of two persons, God and the man assumed by God; he himself, he says, does not hold this, but says that the one who became flesh is not other than the incorporeal one, but the same, in the likeness of our life in the flesh. He goes on to pour out his nonsense to us in incoherent statements. His fleshly God does not have a simple nature, for no one could see simplicity in flesh; and what is not simple cannot be uncompounded. Yet he says that he is one, just as each of us is, made, he says, of spirit, soul and body. Now for the first time we have been taught a new kind of number, learning that things divided into three different kinds are a unit! But let the discussion of the spirit he has invented for him be put off. According to the cruder division of man, as most people divide him, we have been taught to confess that a human being is constituted of a rational soul and a body. How shall we call the two one, when the Apostle clearly sees two men in each of us, where he says, "Even if our outer man is wasting away"—meaning the body—"yet the inner man is being renewed day by day"—alluding to the soul? Indeed, if according to Apolinarius there were three men, he would surely have made two of them invisible and one visible. So even if he props up his own argument by the example of ourselves, calling the two one, Paul overrules him, dividing man into two. Since, then, through the human [example] the account of his doctrine [?]

[?] human, or irrational—that is, if he thinks that man was of a beast's [soul]—and then inserts the rational element into it, which he says is something other than the spirit, calling it "mind" in our case but "God" in his. For if he had first shown us some fashioning of a heavenly man after the likeness of the man of dust, we would have been led along consistently with the myth, learning from this new wisdom that the earthly race of men is constituted of a rational soul and a body, while there is a race of heavenly men whose soul is irrational and whose body is human, and in whom God, instead of a mind, is blended into the combination of body and soul. Apolinarius thinks the one who appeared on earth was made of these. But since that race has neither been shown nor exists, and he who was born through the Virgin is rejected as not having shared our nature, I think it absurd and inconsistent to call what is not a body a body, and what is not a soul a human soul. For if one does not confess the soul to be rational, one will not grant that it is a human soul at all. And if these things are not so, what point is there in that threefold division of the man, of which two-thirds is man and one-third God? "For he would not," he says, "have come to be in the likeness of man unless he were, like a man, an enfleshed mind." Whether the man in whom God reconciled the world to himself was mindless, I cannot say; but that the one who wrote these things was out of his mind at the time he wrote them, the writings themselves cry aloud, even if I do not say it. How does one come to be in the likeness of man who is something other than man and wholly [foreign] to our nature? For if the human compound is a rational soul and a body, and neither this body nor that soul is present in what he has invented, how can what is alien to our nature take on the likeness of man? But he says that he is not a man, but like a man, an enfleshed [?] mind. These are the things that convince me the writer is out of his mind. How can what has no share in a nature be made like that nature? And who is that enfleshed mind? Is it connatural with the flesh and inseparable from it, always being such? Then surely it also comes from such a source? For flesh would not be begotten unless it came from flesh, as the Lord says somewhere: "What is born of the flesh is flesh." Or does it become enfleshed later? Then what sort of flesh does it put on to become enfleshed? Flesh that exists? Then it is from the same [nature as ours]. Flesh that does not exist? Then it is not called enfleshed, for nothing could be named after what does not exist.
But let us look at the inescapable compulsion of his syllogisms, by which [he tries to force] us to agree that the enfleshed [?]

[?] surpassing all understanding, none of the godly would deny, being led to this by the words of the holy Fathers and apostles. For Paul cries out plainly that he "became for us wisdom from God," and that "the saving grace has appeared to us, training us to renounce impiety and, in holiness and righteousness, to await the blessed hope." These things too we have heard the Apostle declare. But that the only-begotten God, who is over all and through all and in all, is an enfleshed mind, we have not heard from any of the saints, nor do we accept inserting this outlandish novelty of language among the divine words—especially when we consider the aim of this new writer. By this frigid piece of sophistry he wants to cast out, in the case of the Lord, the confession of wisdom, through which we believe every mind is made wise, and to bring in instead this irrational novelty of language, so that the Only-begotten may be called an enfleshed mind and not wisdom. "For if," he says, "the Lord is believed to be wisdom—that is, the wisdom present in all who receive grace—we shall no longer confess the coming of Christ as a sojourn of God, since the wisdom would be estranged from God." Who would not pity the man for this melancholy madness? "If we believe him to be wisdom," he says, "then the coming of Christ, who became for us wisdom from God, will not be a sojourn of God but the birth of a man." "If wisdom"? Have you not heard the prophet crying out that "the virgin shall conceive in the womb

and bear a son," and that "a child has been born to us," and that "a Son has the government upon his shoulder," as mighty and powerful, and Father not only of the age that is past but also of the age to come? But let us leave aside this dreamlike drivel, in which he declared that he must be called an enfleshed mind, neither illuminating wisdom nor [one who made] his entry into our life through birth. Another argument: "If the Word did not become an enfleshed mind," he says, "but wisdom..." Here again, what possessed our wise man to set mind against wisdom, as if they were opposites? Those who classify things precisely say that terms set in contrast exclude each other's presence, as life excludes death and death excludes life, as vice excludes virtue and virtue excludes vice, and whatever else is spoken of in the same way. How, then, does this man, equally [?]

…he sets wisdom against mind as opposites, as though the two could not possibly exist in the same thing or belong to the same subject. So he says, "If he was not mind incarnate, he was wisdom." That is like saying, "If it is not health, it is disease." What, then, is his proof? "If wisdom," he says, "was in the mind, the Lord did not descend, nor did he empty himself." What irresistible logic! How does he prove that the Lord did not descend by showing that he was wisdom? If his being wisdom rules out the descent, then whoever confesses the descent must also conclude that he was not wisdom. Now Apolinarius does confess the descent. So he also agrees that the one who descended was not wisdom. Such are the wise arguments this fine fellow makes against the truth. Then, with no coherent connection, he attaches to this premise a proof drawn from premises nobody grants. It runs like this: "For this reason he was also man; for man, according to Paul, is mind in flesh." I ask my readers not to think that I am making these things up as a joke and putting them in Apolinarius's mouth for a laugh. Anyone can see from his own writings that he put this argument forward in exactly these words. So according to which Paul is man called incarnate mind? Let him tell us what other Paul he has hidden away. The servant of Jesus Christ, the one called to be an apostle, said nothing of the kind in anything he wrote. If neither logic nor testimony supports the argument, where does this outlandish piece of dogma-making get its credibility? Next he adds another idea to what he has said: "Since he was man, and heavenly, this is the earthly one [?]." Again I say that he has forgotten Mary. Gabriel brings her the good news. The Holy Spirit is believed to have come upon her, and the power of the Most High overshadows her. From her Jesus is born, who has the dominion upon his shoulder, that is, who bears the Beginning upon himself. And the Beginning is surely God the Word, who was in the beginning and is the beginning, as the word of Scripture says somewhere: "I am the beginning." So either let him show that the Virgin was not on earth, or let him stop fabricating a heavenly man. Nor should he frighten the less educated by suggesting that they sin against the Divine when they accept what is human, not agree[ing] [?] …
[?] … is both man and God: man in what is seen, God in what is understood. But that is not what he says in his conclusion. He places the Divine in what appears, not in what is understood [?] …

But let us move on to the next argument in the treatise. "If, along with God, who is mind," he says, "there was also a human mind in Christ…" That is the premise. To this we reply with a question of our own. Which of the saints ever defined the Divine as mind? From which Scriptures have we been taught that God is the same thing as mind, so that we should accept his claim that the man in Christ is mindless, and that God becomes the mind of what has no mind? Should I copy out the whole disgrace of this argument? I fear that readers would take us for mockers, publishing the writer's indecency to raise a laugh. But so that the premise does not remain incomplete, I need only add the conclusion, and I shall skip the rubbish in between. "If, along with God, who is mind," he says, "there was also a human mind in Christ, then the work of the incarnation is not accomplished in him. But if the work of the incarnation is not accomplished in the self-moved and unconstrained mind, then the work, which is the undoing of sin, is accomplished in the flesh that is moved by another and set in motion by the divine mind. And the self-moved mind in us shares in that undoing to the extent that it makes itself Christ's own." Do you see how well the conclusions fit the premise? Perhaps they need some enchanter and soothsayer to interpret the riddles of these dreams for us and tell us what this novel language means: "the self-moved mind" and "moved by another" and "the flesh that accomplishes the work of undoing." But let these phrases too be left for the young to mock in their high spirits, while we proceed to the rest of the treatise. "If one person gains more than another," he says, "this comes about through training; but there is no training in Christ; therefore there is no human mind." How much does he remember of the divinely inspired Scripture? What training taught Bezalel his crafts? Where did Solomon get his knowledge of so many things? And Amos, who scraped sycamore figs, how did a goatherd come to have such power in prophecy? Yet none of these men came down from heaven, or was in the beginning, or was equal to God.

But let this argument too pass without comment, especially since the conclusion attached to it fits so well. Word for word, it runs: "Therefore the human race is not saved through the taking up of a mind and of a whole man, but through the taking on of flesh." That is the conclusion. As for the difference between "taking up" and "taking on," let it be explained by those who have spent their time on the frigid quibbles of grammar, so that they can lecture schoolboys on the slight difference between such parts of speech, the ones called prepositions. For our part, we hold that what was taken on was taken up, and we have no doubt that what was taken up was taken on, since we have learned this usage from Scripture. "With glory you took me to yourself," says David; and elsewhere, "He chose David his servant and took him up from the flocks of his father." So the one who was taken with glory to himself was taken up, and the one taken up from the flocks was taken to himself, since both things are said of the same person. So what the man means when he says that the mystery of the Only-begotten's becoming man was arranged not by taking up but by taking on, perhaps not even he could tell us. I do not want to plunge my discourse along with his into the mire of his incoherent words, so I pass over most of his drivel. I think that simply reading what he wrote, in his own words, is enough to refute the absurdity of what he says. Even someone eager to attack the heresy as hard as he could would not expose its absurdity by his own reasoning as well as the treatise itself does. For the very arguments by which he builds his falsehood lay bare his impiety through the feebleness of their advocacy. Thus he says, "If perfect God were joined to a perfect man, they would be two." So, in his view, the imperfect joined to the perfect does not count as two. Has this fine fellow never even watched children counting the fingers on their hand? When a child counts the small finger together with the larger one, he calls the smaller one "one" and the greater "one," and yet he says they are two when he reckons them together. For every number is a sum of units and signifies in total what has been collected from them. And if a thing being counted, whatever it is, is set beside another counted with it and exceeds the lesser in size and bulk, the lesser will still be one, even if [?] …

… so we say, but one is deficient and the other perfect. Yet this great authority on arithmetic says that if each is perfect in its own nature, the things so described are called two; but if one is deficient and the other perfect, the two become one. I do not know how he smears the imperfect together with what is superabundant and contrives a union of incompatible things by means of their contraries. For by likeness, perfect fits better with perfect, and imperfect with imperfect. So let the lawgiver of this new arithmetic tell us how contrary is united with contrary, I mean the imperfect with the perfect. But he does not think it fitting to conceive of a human mind in the Only-begotten God, and he gives the reason: the human mind is changeable. Then by the same argument he should not grant God flesh either. Not even the writer would deny that flesh is changeable, since it changes from youth to maturity, putting on one age after another like garments. Or how was he not changeable, who was first carried in his mother's arms, then grew to be a child, then a youth, and so advanced little by little to maturity until he reached the full measure of human stature? If the mind is rejected because it is changeable, then for the same reason he should not allow the flesh either. And so, on his view, the whole Gospel will be shown to be false, the preaching empty and faith vain. But if no one doubts that he was manifested in the flesh, and changeable flesh at that, then there is no reason at all to reject the mind on the same grounds. Just as he was not defiled by coming in the flesh, so too he was not altered and changed by taking on a mind. Let me take up his argument again, setting out his statement word for word: "Therefore," he says, "the human race is not saved through the taking up of a mind and of a whole man, but through the taking on of flesh, which by nature is meant to be governed. And it needed an unchangeable mind, one that would not fall under its control through weakness of knowledge, but would fit it to itself without compulsion." Who does not know that what is needy is entirely different in nature from what lacks nothing, and that what is by nature governed is different from what by nature rules? They differ in the very principle of their being, just as the nature of irrational animals was made to be subject to human nature, and man's rule over irrational animals is not acquired but his own by nature. If, then, it is natural for the flesh to be

governed, as Apolinarius says, and the Divine is by nature governing, how can the one who grants this declare that the two were one in nature from the beginning? It is plain to everyone that what is subject has one principle and what presides has another, and that what is by nature led is one thing and what by nature governs is another. If the nature of each, I mean of the flesh and of the Godhead, is seen in opposite properties, how are the two natures one? And how can he fashion a divine and heavenly flesh around the Word? Or rather, he makes the Word flesh beforehand: not someone who entered our form in the last days by the divine plan, but someone who always was this and always remained in that same state. For whoever says that the flesh needs the unchangeable and requires a guide is plainly speaking of our flesh, which fell into sin through the changeability of its nature. But if, as he says, a supercelestial and divine body is to be seen in the Word, then to be consistent he cannot ascribe changeability to it, nor any need of someone to direct it. And this is not our word but that of the divine voice, which said that the healthy do not need a physician, but the sick do. For in heaven there is no sickness that comes from sin. It is we who fell sick with sin, we who grew weak by letting evil in. It is we who, by turning to evil, came to need the unchangeable, and we who wandered from the road of salvation and came to need a guide to the good. So if the writer is right to attribute these things to the Lord's flesh, that it is by nature governed and needs an unchangeable guide, then all his account describes is our own composite nature. But if he places the Godhead in the flesh, then the Divine, being what it is called, needs no one else to guide it, for it admits no change or alteration for the worse. In that case, all he has just said about the flesh has been recited in vain. For if this flesh is somehow divine, it is clearly unchangeable; and if it is changeable, it is certainly not divine.

Who could go through this confused and incoherent tale of doctrines, which never holds the same ground but, like the images of a dream, appears now as one thing and now as another? At one moment he says that the flesh of the Word is divine and coeternal. Then it is acquired and taken on. Then it is foreign to our nature, which is subject to suffering and death. Then again it needs someone to direct it and is subject to change and alteration. For this reason he makes it mindless, so that it may be healed by the Godhead, as though he thought that the mind gets in the way of God's care for human beings and that mindlessness is dearer to God. Then he must think it more blessed to have no mind, if indeed, as he says, God takes on what is mindless. Why, then, does he not correct Solomon, who says, "The man of understanding will acquire the art of steering"? I do not think the riddle of the proverb means any other steering here than that of our nature, tossed by the storms of evil and shipwrecked, being steered by the true helmsman into the harbor of the divine will. If man is saved by mindlessness, how will the man of understanding acquire steering? And to which of our parts would the Divine be more akin by nature? To which does reason suppose the divine nature to correspond more closely? The flesh is something gross and resistant, akin to the nature of the earth. The intellect is something spiritual, invisible and without shape. Of these, which would be found more fit to be joined to God: the gross and earthy, or the intangible and shapeless? And how can flesh be joined to God "without compulsion," as he says, and share in pure virtue? Who does not know that virtue is an achievement of free choice? The flesh is the instrument of choice. It lies subject to the impulse of the intellect and is moved toward whatever the mover leads it to. And choice is nothing else than a kind of mind, a disposition toward something. So if he says that the man in whom there is no mind shares in pure virtue, what is it that willingly receives that virtue? Unless the writer takes what is compelled to be uncompelled. For whenever the body stays clear of evil deeds without the mind assenting to the better inclination, whatever is achieved will be the work of necessity, not of choice. But whoever chooses the good by weighing his reasonings is superior to all necessity and force, since the inclination to the better comes from within him. How, then, can the writer credit freedom from compulsion to what has no choice, when no reasoning of its own has guided it to the good? For sinlessness that does not come from [?] …

choice is not praiseworthy at all. Otherwise we would also praise those whom chains keep from crime, since it is the chain that keeps them from doing evil, not their will. "But without compulsion," he says, "the Godhead draws the flesh to itself." Clearly by "without compulsion" he means "voluntarily." How, then, could anyone be drawn willingly to virtue without having a will of his own? Choosing, willing, selecting what is beneficial and rejecting what is harmful all belong to the intellect, and thinking does not belong to the mindless. So if the flesh is joined to God without compulsion, the writer's own words testify that the flesh does not lack choice, and that it holds to what is profitable with judgment and deliberation. No one would call that irrational. How could reason exist in what is irrational? So by his own words he concedes not only that there is a mind in this man, but that it surpasses all others. For a voluntary and uncompelled impulse toward the good testifies to the perfection of the mind. That being drawn to the better belongs to the intellect is shown especially by what he says next, which runs word for word: "For it imparts pure virtue to every mind subject to it." If, then, he sees purity of virtue in the mind, how can he banish the mind from the flesh in which he sees that purity? One of the two must be a mistake in his argument: either that the mind shares in virtue, or that the flesh drawn to virtue without compulsion is mindless. What he added, disconnected and inconsequent as it is, I think it superfluous to examine. It runs like this: "And to all who are made like Christ in mind [?], and not made unlike him in the flesh." Let the admirers of this deceit explain what such nauseating stuff means; we shall proceed to the rest of the treatise. "And if God," he says, "were joined to a man, perfect to perfect, they would be two: one Son of God by nature, and one by adoption." I would gladly learn from those who are schooled in such things: if they call the intelligent and perfect man an adopted son, what will they call the mindless man, as they must call one who has no mind? For the only-begotten God, being in himself complete and perfect, bears the name of true Son, [?] confirming …

… and the half-complete man, insofar as he is man, will obviously be called a half-adopted son, since in him the title of adopted son is cut in half. So it would be more accurate to say that the one is the perfect adopted son, while this one falls short by half, or by a third, as those who mince up man with such divisions please. But if it is unfitting for God to have an adopted son, it is surely just as unfitting whether the son is perfect or imperfect; or rather, the absurdity is even greater in the case of the mutilated one. For if it was thought shameful, and contrary to any notion worthy of God, that the wholeness of human nature should be seen in the Divine, it would be far more shameful to see a maimed nature in him. The flesh is not akin to the Father's nature just because it has no mind. Rather, the whole man and his part alike are separated from the Father's essence by the principle of their nature, and nothing in us, neither the mind nor the body, is akin in essence to the nature that transcends us. Even if his myth fashions some heavenly kind of flesh around the Divine, no reasonable person will on that account be any readier to agree that this flesh is of one essence with God the Father. But if the flesh is foreign to the Father's essence, how could what is foreign be Son? For it is absolutely necessary that whatever truly comes from something should be in essence what its begetter is. But the Father is not flesh. So neither could what comes from him be flesh at all; for what is born of the Spirit is said to be spirit, and not flesh. If, then, the flesh is not from the Father, it is not Son. What, then, will it be called? Whatever name they devise for that heavenly flesh invented by the writer, we shall consistently give to the flesh taken up from humankind; and whatever they call ours, theirs will be called by the same name. If the earthly flesh is not Son, then neither is the other. If the earthly is an adopted son, then so is the other. If there are two sons here, there are surely two there as well. If in their case the flesh and the Godhead are one Son, the same holds here too. For since all creation stands equally far from the divine essence, it is agreed that the earthly and the heavenly alike are outside the Father's nature. What remains is to believe about God whatever better accords with the purpose of his love for humankind: that the flesh finds no name of its own, but is named together with what predominates and prevails. It is like what happens in the sea: if someone drops a drop of vinegar into the sea, the drop too becomes sea …

…becomes, being transformed along with the quality of the sea. In the same way the true Son and only-begotten God, the unapproachable light, life itself, wisdom and sanctification and power, and every lofty name and idea: all these he is who was manifested to human beings through flesh. The flesh was flesh by its own nature, but it was transformed into the ocean of incorruption, as the Apostle says, "What is mortal was swallowed up by life." So everything then seen in the flesh was transformed along with it into the divine and pure nature. Its weight, form, colour, solidity and softness, its limits of size, and everything else seen in it at that time no longer remain, because the blending with the Divine has taken up the lowliness of the fleshly nature into the divine properties. So there is no danger that our doctrine of the Trinity will be enlarged into a tetrad, as Apollinarius says. Nor do we enslave the angels to a man, as his fable claims against us. Those who bow before the Master are not serving a man, and they are not ashamed to worship the one who visited the world through flesh. For "when he brings the firstborn into the world," it says, "he says, 'Let all his angels worship him.'" There is only one way into the world, which is birth, and no one can enter human life without using this way in. So Scripture calls his birth in the flesh his entry into the world. If, then, all the angels worship him when he enters the world, and his entry is birth through flesh, we are not enslaving to the Master his own possession. Rather, the nature of the angels itself is well aware of the lordship that stands above it. So let him be silent who puts these empty words into his treatise: "We turn things upside down by enslaving God-bearing angels to a God-bearing man." Besides this he says: "If the one who received God…"

…reconciling [the world] to himself." The great Paul is a sufficient witness to this. But the writer supposes that we introduce a multitude of gods into the gospel, because we confess that God in Christ was reconciling the world to himself, since God came to be among human beings as well. To this we make the following defence. Suppose there were many mothers who were virgins, and Gabriel brought his message to many of them, and the Holy Spirit came upon each one, and the power of the Most High was present to each. Suppose the prophets proclaimed the grace of many, so that they said in the plural, "Children have been born to us" (and "sons have been given to us"), and "The virgins shall conceive," and all those born were named Emmanuel. Suppose all of them walked on foot over the waves, and by an inexpressible power fed so many thousands in the desert, making the bread multiply in the hands of the disciples until all were full. Suppose all of them raised men four days dead out of their graves. Suppose all of them became lambs of God, were sacrificed as a Passover for us, nailed sin to the cross, destroyed the power of death, rose up to heaven before the disciples' eyes, and sat at the right hand of the Father. Suppose all of them will come to judge the world in righteousness, and every tongue of those in heaven, on earth and under the earth confesses in the name of all of them. Then we will grant that there are many gods, since the many would bear these distinguishing marks. But if there is one Lord Jesus, through whom all things exist, and from whom and through whom and to whom are all things, and if this whole list of attributes befitting God belongs to him alone, what danger is there of inventing many gods when we say that God was manifested through ensouled flesh? Who is so ignorant of the Gospel teachings as not to know that what was seen was a man? The Saviour himself said to the Jews, "But now you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth." You see in these words what it was that he pointed to as the one being killed. When he said, "You seek to kill me," he meant not the truth but the man through whom the truth spoke. For it was not a man who was speaking the truth. Clearly the one speaking was God, while the man passed on to human beings, in his own voice, what was said. That is why he also became the mediator between God and human beings. Human nature cannot enter into unmixed communion with God, and therefore it needs a voice that is akin to it and natural to it, through which the power from above can fittingly be received. But this too we must leave, and turn our argument to what comes next. "Nothing," he says, [Notes: (6) Corrected reading: "we reply." (9) Corrected reading: "in the eyes." [?] Gen. 45.]

"…is so united to God as the flesh that was assumed." What a carefully considered statement! Nothing is so united to God as the flesh: not goodness, not eternity, not incorruption, not power over all things, nor any other attribute befitting God. All these come second to the flesh in their relation to God, and in God's union with it, the flesh that was acquired. The writer himself admits this very point, for by saying that it was assumed he showed that it was created. We will pass over what follows in silence, since it carries its own refutation of this incoherent fable-making and can do readers no harm. He first stated that nothing else said of God is as united to the Lord as the assumed flesh is united to him. Then in his conclusion he added that things not so united are not so worthy of worship, and he crowned it all with this: "Nothing is so worthy of worship as the flesh of Christ." Let us pass over these things, and their meaning, in silence, for their absurdity is plain even to children. Even children sitting and playing in the marketplaces would say: "If nothing is as worthy of worship as the flesh, then the flesh of Christ is more to be revered than the majesty of the Father himself, his almighty authority, his rule over all things, and whatever else our nature can say about the divine power. So we should stop worshipping the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and revere and worship only the flesh that this man ranks above them, and grant it power over all things." His next argument is like the earlier ones: "The flesh of the Lord," he says, "is worshipped insofar as it is one person and one living being with him." He mentioned two things, the Lord and the Lord's flesh, and made the two into one living being. Now he openly reveals what the title of his treatise points to, in which he professes to teach about the divine incarnation as being "in the likeness of man." For since to the body of a soul [?]… [Notes: (17) Corrected reading: "created in addition, as he admits." (18) Corrected reading: "and this too we will pass over," and [?]…]
[Notes: (20) Corrected reading: "we will pass over in silence along with their folly"; and shortly after [?]. (21) Corrected reading: "and in that."]

…right away, in the title of his treatise, he professes to teach that the Divine too is seen in flesh in the likeness of a human being. Now, in this part of the treatise, he plainly sets out to prove that the flesh and the Lord are one person and one living being. It is as if he were saying that the visible Paul is the same as the hidden Paul, because body and soul are joined in one nature. Why, then, should we pursue and fight against these statements? Would no one accuse us of folly for opposing such made-up notions? So let us look at what comes next. "If no creature is worshipped with the Lord as his flesh is." Who will judge the contest between Apollinarius and Eunomius as they compete for first prize in impiety? Which of them will be awarded the prize for their labours against the truth? Perhaps the victory will be left undecided between them, since they are so closely matched in impiety. Eunomius calls the only-begotten God a creature, but he does not deny that he is spiritual and free of solid, material nature. Apollinarius, from the beginning, fashions him as a compound of different natures and argues that he is one living being assembled from flesh and Godhead, in the likeness of human nature. Both alike worship a creature. But Eunomius says it was a spiritual and incorporeal nature that was made, while Apollinarius adds that the creature has a fleshly nature, and that this is worshipped more than other creatures. This implies that worship is offered to other creatures as well, which even the champions of Eunomius' views admit is impious. So let Apollinarius carry off the prize of victory over Eunomius, and let him exult, adorned with the crowns of impiety. In human nature the body is inferior to the soul. By the same measure, among those who worship creatures, the one who decrees that the flesh is to be worshipped is more absurd in his impiety than those who revere a spiritual creature. This is all the more so if he says that other creatures are worshipped too, and that the flesh surpasses them by comparison in the worship it receives. "For no creature," he says, "is as worthy of worship as the flesh of the Lord." Everything found in creation, whether incorporeal or bodily, is equally beneath the divine power. But within creation itself there is, by comparison, higher and lower, and incorporeal nature ranks above the sensible and bodily condition. So insofar as Eunomius and Apollinarius both think a creature ought to be worshipped, they are evenly matched in impiety and the contest is undecided. But the one who gives first place to the flesh over spiritual nature has the greater share of impiety. Let the disciples of this deception hear whom their teacher is competing against, and over what. [Notes: (28) So corrected; previously "ἀμφορίστῳ." (34) So corrected; previously "προπορευούσης."]

Let us look [?] next at the fetter that follows, to borrow a phrase from Apollinarius' own teacher, which he presents bound tight with the unbreakable chains of his syllogisms. "If," he says, "someone thinks that a man is united to God beyond all men and angels…" Must we examine the meaning of these words too? It would be like looking for a soul in a stone or wisdom in a block of wood to look in the words quoted for any trace of thought. I do not mean a better thought, but even one that served the cause of impiety. Rather, the context will show that what he says is unintelligible. "He will make angels and men not free, just as the flesh is not free. But for a free living being, not being free is destruction. And a nature is not destroyed by the one who made it. Therefore a man is not united to God." What compelling logic! How unbreakable the coils of his syllogisms! Union with the Divine takes free will away from men and angels. For a free living being, not being free means destruction. And if he posits these things, it is proved that a man is not united to God. What ventriloquist ever said anything like this? What do those who speak from the ground, and are trained in divination from the belly, babble that comes close to it? "Freedom is taken away from men and angels if humanity is united to God." Was it not a man who said, "But now you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth"? Was he not blended with the divine nature, he who all [?]… [Note: (37) Corrected reading: "but rather it may be…"]

Does he not count slaves among living beings, then, because they do not order their lives freely but are enslaved to the power that rules over them? For the writer defines a living being by its having free will. Whoever lacks a will that moves on its own authority, he decrees, should not be thought a living being at all. In that case Canaan was dead when he was made a slave to his brothers for his misconduct. Abraham's servant was dead, Gehazi, Elisha's servant, was dead, and in later times Onesimus was dead. All centurions who serve under orders are dead. But why list these? All who are yoked under the rule of those in power, whose free will is restricted, are dead. Even those whom Paul commands to be subject to the governing authorities are surely dead, even though they are living souls, destroyed by the absence of free will and no longer able to be living beings. This is what Apollinarius' fable requires, so that he can yoke that soulless flesh to the God who is over all. Whether it is soulless or mindless makes no difference, for the fable looks equally to both. But what is soulless is a corpse, and what has a soul but no mind is a beast. He does not even shrink from this as absurd, since he takes free will away from that flesh. For it is characteristic of irrational animals not to be their own masters but to be subject to human rule.

But let these points go too, and let us move on to the next part of his treatise. For brevity's sake I will state my opponent's meaning in my own words. He says that a human being is made of three parts, spirit, soul and body, as the Apostle teaches in his Epistle to the Thessalonians. He adds this part of the hymn of the Three Young Men: "Bless the Lord, you spirits and souls of the righteous." Then he cites "to serve the Lord in spirit," and quotes the words of the Gospel which teach us that those who worship God must worship in spirit. Having gone through these, he adds that there is something besides this, the flesh that wars against the spirit. He says this flesh is not without a soul, so that the spirit is thereby shown to be a third thing besides the soul and the body. "If, then," he says, "a human being is made of three parts, and the Lord too is a man, then the Lord is certainly also made of three parts: spirit, soul and body." To make clear how mistaken his understanding of the divine Scriptures is, we will briefly take up each of the points he has made. And first let us examine the Apostle's words. For it is not [Note: (46) Corrected reading: "song."]

…as though he were dividing a human being into three sections, in our view, that Paul writes to the Thessalonians, praying that they may be wholly sanctified for the Lord in body, soul and spirit. Rather, he has a far loftier philosophy concerning the choice of how to live in this life, not only here but also where he addresses the Corinthians. There he recognizes one person who is fleshly, another who is spiritual, and between the two, one who is soul-driven [psychic]. He calls fleshly the one who is ruled by passions and bound to matter. He names spiritual the one who is not weighed down by the drag of the body but keeps his mind on high things. And he calls soul-driven the one who is neither of these strictly and has a share in both. In saying this, he does not claim that the fleshly person lacks the activity of mind or soul. He does not present the spiritual person as cut off from union with body and soul. Nor does he suppose that the soul-driven person has no mind or no flesh. He simply gives these names to people's moral choices according to what predominates in them. The one who judges all things and is judged by no one has flesh and soul and is still called spiritual. The man who, driven mad by the passion of the flesh, defiled his father's bed was neither soulless nor without a mind. Likewise the one in the middle, who has something both of what is praiseworthy and of what is condemned, partakes of both: he has a mind within him and is clothed in the nature of flesh. But, as has been said, the names properly fit the visible marks of a person's life. The self-indulgent, the pleasure-lovers, and those who throw themselves passionately into quarrels and rivalries are called fleshly. Those who judge all things but give no handle to anyone who wants to judge them are called spiritual because of the loftiness of their conduct. And he calls soul-driven the one who stands between these, who falls as far short of the one as he rises above the other. He wants the one who is being perfected through virtue not only to be known for his lofty life, but also to look to God whenever he does anything bodily, and not to fall away from God even when he does things that are morally indifferent. "Whether you eat," he says, "or drink, or whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God," so that even in bodily occupations we do not lose sight of the goal of God's glory. For this reason, to the [Notes: (50) Corrected reading: "having been precise, and toward." (52) Corrected reading: "falls short of this one as much as." (53) The copyist had omitted "anything."]

…[Apol]linarius [thinks] that by this the mind is blessed in particular, and the body and the soul each separately, so that the force of the blessing on each of them is distinguished. But then how is the body kept whole, when it will utterly and inevitably fall apart in death? How is a body kept whole when it is pressed down and shrivelled by self-control and worn out by harsh discipline? How could anyone say that poor Lazarus did not miss out on the blessing, covered as he was with sores and wasting away from their discharge? Yet, paradoxical as it may sound, in that body running with sores Paul's blessing was fulfilled completely. His body was kept whole together with his soul through his spiritual way of life, because the needs of the flesh did not drag him down from his higher hope into any unworthy thought. His flesh did not distract his soul, and his mind was not troubled [?] by bodily passions. The hymn of the Three Young Men, too, which calls the spirits and souls of the righteous to join in giving glory, does not command the souls to praise on their own and the spirits on their own apart from the souls, as Apollinarius thinks. What praise could belong to the soul alone that was not accomplished through the mind? For a soul cut off from mind, as has already been said many times, is a beast with no share in rational and intellectual activity. Why, then, does he separate the mind from our soul, as he says? Let it be granted that praise can be offered to God by the spirits, since he says the spirits are mind. But if he thinks the soul is something other than mind, how will the mindless praise God? Who will please God with a hymn sung mindlessly? And what further need would the soul have of mind, if it were sufficient by itself to sing hymns in glorifying God and needed no help from the mind? But this is not what we have learned from those who have interpreted Scripture for us. Rather, souls freed from the bonds of the body are equal to the angels, as the Lord says. So by pairing souls with spirits, the text shows that souls share equal honour with the angels. For the angels are spirits, according to the prophet who said, "He makes his angels spirits," and it is with them that the Three Young Men call the souls of the righteous to sing as well. And when the Saviour says that God must be worshipped in spirit, he does not mean the mind by the word "spirit"; he means that we must not hold any bodily [Notes: 1 Thess. 5:23. Luke 20:36. …notions about the Divine. The Samaritan woman told the Lord that God must be worshipped on the mountain, as though he were confined to a place, and this is not free of a bodily conception. So the Word tells the woman who had strayed from the truth that God is spirit, that is, incorporeal. Those who worship him cannot approach the incorporeal in a bodily way, but must offer their worship in spirit and truth. He sets these corrective words against her twofold ignorance, opposing truth to the type and spirit to bodily notions. This is why Paul too says that we serve the Lord neither in a type nor in the body but in spirit, following the truth. And the statement that "the flesh does not submit to the law of God" carries within itself the refutation of their deceptive doctrine. For waging war, taking captive, refusing to submit, and all such things are acts of the will, and without a mind there would be no will. So the flesh that Apollinarius calls ensouled and endowed with will is, by his own admission, not without a mind either. Even if it is called simply "flesh," it contains within itself the whole definition of humanity, since nothing can be called a human being if any of the components of that nature is missing. [?]…receptacle. There is much obscurity in what he has said, and it is hard to pin down because his expression is so feeble. Still, his intent is easy to uncover. He says that if that man was deficient in mind, he is heavenly; but if he was complete, he is no longer heavenly but has become a receptacle of the heavenly God. Which of these statements should we loathe more? Is it the notion that the Divine is hampered by [?]rarefaction, as though the flesh were more suited than the mind to union with the Godhead? Or is it the belief that God is heavenly, while the one who received the heavenly God into himself is not where God is believed to be but somewhere other than heaven, and is called by some other name? For if, as Apollinaris says, he is a receptacle of the heavenly God, and God is in heaven above, as Ecclesiastes says, then the one who has contained God within himself is with the one he contains, and is properly called heavenly instead of earthly. So even by the writer's own words, had he understood where they lead, the doctrine of truth is clearly established and strengthened by the wisdom of its enemies. But let us examine what follows. "But if we," he says, "are made of three, and he of four, he is not a man but a Man-God." The reader should not laugh at how silly and senseless the expression looks. Let him groan instead at the willful blindness of those enslaved to this absurdity. If the whole of human nature is saved by the indwelling of the divine power, then God the Word will be named "Man-God." The myths weave together different natures and conjure up monstrous creatures, shapes and names, fashioning and naming horse-stags, goat-stags and the like. In the same way the new mythmaker, following his teachers in the art of poetry, makes a mockery of the divine mystery. Yet the Apostle cries out plainly, "Through a man came the resurrection of the dead." He does not mean half a man, nor one with a little more than half, but by the unqualified word he shows that the nature signified by the name is undiminished. This man, however, turns the mystery into a minotaur for us with his shameful coinage, and by what he has said he gives those outside the faith many pretexts for mocking the word of faith. For anyone who wants to ridicule our doctrines for a laugh cannot be turned away from discussing this absurd compound,

whether the writer's view or ours seems to prevail. Whichever of the two you assert, you will not remove from the account a composition out of two natures. Whoever said that the flesh is from above did not thereby establish that it is not flesh. And flesh governed by some animate nature, with a vital power in itself, as Apollinaris would also have it, properly bears the name "man." But the one who assumed it, and manifested himself through it, is wholly different from it in nature. The very word "assumption" shows that what assumes differs in nature from what is assumed. Even if these points hold, then, what will prevent God, who was manifested in the flesh, from being insulted by that absurd coinage, so that the one so constituted is called "Man-God," as Apollinaris boldly puts it? For the myth did not give the goat-stag its name because the goat part grew in half measure onto a whole stag, or because the animals were mixed the other way round, so that the stag part grew onto an entire goat. The compound name expresses that it shares in each nature in some way or other. So by the writer's own reasoning, if the same one is both man and God, joined in any way at all, whether the whole nature comes together or is present only in part, he will not escape that absurd compound name. And if the Greeks learn these things from him and turn our mystery into comedy, the one who gave them occasion for blasphemy will surely fall under the prophetic curse that says, "Woe to him through whom my name is blasphemed among the nations." Let us consider what he goes on to add. "If he is made of two perfect things," he says, "then he is not man in that in which he is God, nor God in that in which he is man." But suppose it is granted that the compound is made of a deficient thing and a perfect one, as he argues. Will not those who dare such statements say the same thing, that in that in which he is God he is not man, and in that in which he is man he is not God? For the definition of Godhead and the definition of manhood are different in every way, and no one would [have represented] the diminution (85) Correction: ἐν ἀψύχῳ. of the nature by this word. The meaning of the words suffers no confusion, such that one would understand the one name in the other. Neither is the one signified in the other nor the other in the one. Each name keeps its natural meaning, and their senses will in no way be interchanged. "Imperfect" and "perfect," however, put quite different notions before the hearer. We call perfect what is complete according to the proper definition of its nature, and imperfect the opposite. Neither word, said by itself, signifies man or God. Whatever thing or name it is joined to, it leads us to think of what is meant as either full or deficient. How, then, does Apollinaris establish that if the man was imperfect, the imperfect is God, as though the mutilation of our nature agreed with the definition of Godhead? Advancing his argument again to the next point, he says: "One who is merely a man, subject to the common corruption of men, cannot save the world." I say this too. If human nature were sufficient to secure the good for itself, the mystery would be superfluous. But it was impossible to escape death unless God provided salvation. That is why the light shines in the darkness through flesh, to banish through flesh the destruction that comes from darkness. "But neither are we saved by God," he says, "unless he is mingled with us." In these words the writer seems to be in his right mind and to bring his soul back to sensible reasoning, for whoever speaks of mixture signifies the union of things that differ by nature. "And he is mingled," he says, "having become flesh, that is, man, as the Gospel says that when he became flesh, then he dwelt among us." Not even this is out of tune with sound doctrine, unless he later sows some tares beside it. For this is our account, or rather the account of the truth: he dwelt among us when he became flesh, and conversely, he became flesh when he dwelt among us. If, then, the flesh dates from his dwelling among us, the Word was not yet flesh before Gabriel brought the good news to the Virgin. And that man is false who says that the human element came down to us from above (and that the man existed before human nature), the man through whom the divine was mingled with human life. "But neither does he loose the sin of men," he says, "unless he became a sinless man, nor (94) Correction: διὰ τῶν λεγομένων. (97) Correction: ἀλλ' ὅπερ. I read ἀλλ' ᾧπερ. (98) Correction: ἐλλιπές. does he destroy the reign of death over all men unless he died as a man and rose again." If only he had kept his good sense to the end and spoken the Church's language! But he turns back to his own views and finds fault with the Church's teaching that we regard the passion as belonging to the man. To refute our view he adds his own argument, which runs as follows: "The death of a man," he says, "does not abolish death." What is he trying to establish by saying this? That the very Godhead of the Only-begotten, truth itself, life itself, was put to death in the passion of the cross. Then, during that span of three days, there was no life, no power, no righteousness, no light, no truth, not even the Godhead itself. He does not say that when one Godhead died another was left, since in many places he is seen fighting Arius on this very point and arguing that the Godhead of the Trinity is one. If that Godhead was put to death, as his argument implies, there was certainly no other. How anyone could suppose that he does not make the Godhead mortal, I cannot see. What else is death in a man but the dissolution of what is composite? In us, when the body is dissolved into the elements it is made of, the soul does not perish along with it. The composite is dissolved, but what is not composite remains undissolved. If, then, death does not touch the soul, how is the Godhead put to death? Let those who do not know what they are saying answer that. I will pass over the passages that come next, insofar as they belong to the same argument. In what follows he tries to establish that the Godhead of the Only-begotten itself died, saying that "the death of a man does not abolish death, nor does one rise who has not died. From all this," he says, "it is clear that God himself died, inasmuch," he says, "as it was not possible for Christ to be held by death." Their absurdity is plain, so I think these statements should be passed over without examination. Anyone with sense can see for himself how impious and absurd it is to declare outright that God himself died, having undergone death in his own nature. Still, it is perhaps reasonable to point out this much: even what he puts into our mouths is not free of falsehood. Some of it has been slanderously invented to discredit our teaching. He claims that we say Christ did not exist from the beginning, in the way that the Word is God. We do not deny that in the last days the power of God, the wisdom, the light and the life, all of which Christ is, were manifested through flesh. But to say that these once did not exist, and that the one (9) Correction: τοῦ τε νοῦν ἔχοντος, καὶ ἀφ' ἑαυτοῦ συνιδεῖν.

who is signified and named by them, Lord and Christ, did not exist, is in our judgment no less impious than denying the name altogether. For whoever says that Christ did not exist from the beginning (and Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God and every lofty name befitting God) cannot say that anything else exists that is understood by this great name. The designation "man" includes rationality, the capacity for knowledge, and any other property said to mark the nature. If someone says that man does not exist, the other properties of the nature are wholly abolished along with the rejection of the name. In the same way, Christ is the power, the wisdom, the imprint, the radiance. Whoever says that he did not exist from the beginning will surely also reject everything conceived together with him. That is why, guided by the holy Scriptures, we say that Christ always exists and is contemplated together with the eternity of the Father. The only-begotten God is always God. He does not become this by participation, nor does he pass by some progress from a lower state to Godhead. In the same way the power, the wisdom and every name befitting God are co-eternal with the Godhead, so that nothing that was not there from the beginning is added to the glory of the nature. And we say that the name of Christ in particular has been contemplated in the Only-begotten from eternity, since the very meaning of the name leads us to this view. To confess this name is to hold the doctrine of the holy Trinity, for each of the persons in whom we believe is fittingly indicated by this designation. Lest we seem to be saying anything of our own, we will set out the words of the prophecy: "Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; the scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated lawlessness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions." In these words the throne signifies rule over all. The scepter of uprightness expresses the impartiality of judgment. The oil of gladness represents the power of the Holy Spirit, with which God is anointed by God, that is, the Only-begotten by the Father, because he loved righteousness and hated injustice. Suppose there was a time when he was not a friend of righteousness and an enemy of injustice. Then it would follow that he was once not anointed either, since he is said to have been anointed because he loved righteousness and hated injustice. But he is always a friend of righteousness, for he would never hate himself, being righteousness itself. Clearly, then, he is always seen in the anointing as well. Just as the righteous man is not unrighteous, so the Anointed would never be unanointed, and one who is never unanointed is surely always anointed. That the (11) Correction: τοῦτο γίνεται. anointer is the Father and the anointing is the Holy Spirit, everyone would agree, at least anyone whose heart is not covered by the Jewish veil. How, then, can he say that we hold that Christ did not exist from the beginning? It is not that, because we confess Christ to be eternal, we also think of the flesh he formed as always belonging to him. Rather, we know the same one as both Christ and Lord before the ages, and after the passion we confess this very thing again, as Peter says to the Jews: "God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified." We say this not because we see a pair of Christs and Lords in the one. The only-begotten God is God by nature, Lord of all, king of all creation, maker of all that exists and restorer of what has fallen. In his great patience he chose not to thrust our nature, fallen through sin, away from fellowship with himself, but to receive it back into life. And he himself is the life. So at the end of human history, when our wickedness had grown to its height, he accepted the mingling with the lowliness of our nature, so that no part of evil might be left unhealed. He took man into himself and himself came to be in man, as he says to the disciples, "I in you and you in me." What he himself was, he made the one blended with him to be as well. He himself was always most high above all, and so he exalted what was lowly; the one who is most high above all certainly did not need to be exalted further. The Word was Christ and Lord, and this is what the one mingled with him and taken up into the Godhead also becomes. For the one who is Lord is not appointed to lordship a second time; rather, the form of the servant becomes Lord. That is why it is said, "One Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things." In the same way Christ, who before the ages was clothed in the glory of the Spirit (this is what the anointing signifies through symbols), adorns the man united to him with the same anointing after the passion and makes him Christ. "For glorify me," he says, (15) Correction: ὁ Πατήρ. (17) So corrected; previously, wrongly, πάλιν τε αὐτὸν τοῦτον ὁμολογούμενον. (18) Previously it read τὸ κατὰ τὴν ἡμετέραν. The teaching of true religion hands down the holy Trinity as existing before the ages. "He who exists before the ages," the prophecy says of the Father. Of the Only-begotten the Apostle says, "Through him the ages were made." And the glory before the ages that is contemplated around the only-begotten God is the Holy Spirit. What belonged to Christ, who was with the Father before the world existed, comes at the end of the ages to belong also to what was united to Christ. For it says, "Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit." So let him not slander our teaching as though we said that the only-begotten God is not always Christ. He is always Christ, both before the economy of salvation and after it. But he is man neither before it nor after, only during the time of the economy. The man did not exist before the Virgin, and after the ascension into heaven the flesh no longer remains in its own properties. "For even if we once knew Christ according to the flesh," it says, "we no longer know him so." Because God was manifested in flesh, it does not follow that he remained flesh. The human is changeable and the divine unchangeable. So the Godhead cannot be moved by any change and is not altered toward the worse (for it does not admit the worse, and nothing is better than it). The human nature in Christ, by contrast, has undergone change for the better. It has been altered from corruptible to incorruptible, from perishable to imperishable, from short-lived to everlasting, from bodily and shaped to bodiless and shapeless. They say that we claim it was the man who suffered, not God. Let them hear this from us: we confess that the Godhead was in the one who suffered, but not that the impassible nature became subject to suffering. To make this clearer, we hold the following

view. Human nature has its subsistence from an intellectual soul joined to a body. The two together grow from a material starting point laid down beforehand for their constitution. That matter becomes a man when divine power gives it life and form. If one supposed, for the sake of argument, that God's creative power was not present to constitute what is being formed, the matter would surely remain inert and motionless, since the creative activity would not bring it to life. In our case, then, a life-giving power is seen in the matter from which a man, composed of soul and body, is fashioned. In the same way, in the virgin birth, the power of the Most High was implanted immaterially, through the life-giving Spirit, in an undefiled body. It made the Virgin's incorruption the material of the flesh and received what the virginal body contributed to the one being formed. So the truly new man was created, the first and only one to show in himself this mode of subsistence. He was created according to God, not according to man. The divine power pervaded the whole nature of the compound equally, so that neither part lacked a share in the Godhead. It was in both, in soul, I mean, and in body, present in each naturally and fittingly. When the man was born, the Godhead did not need to be born, for it exists before all ages and remains forever. But having once come to be in the man at his constitution, it also appeared together with him at his birth. In the same way, what lives forever does not need to rise. It rises in the one brought back to life by the divine power. It is not raised itself (for it had not fallen), but raises in itself the one who had fallen. If, then, the Divine needs neither birth nor resurrection, the passion too is clearly accomplished not as though the Godhead suffered. The Godhead was in the one who suffered, and through its union with the sufferer it made his suffering its own. As has been said, the divine nature was implanted fittingly in both soul and body and became one with each. And since "the gifts of God are irrevocable," as Scripture says, it withdraws from neither of them but remains forever. Nothing separates anyone from union with God except sin, and where a life is sinless, its union with God is entirely inseparable. (32) Correction: μηδέτερον. (33) Correction: ἐν ἑκατέρῳ. …the presence of the divine nature. When death had separated the soul from the body, what was composite was divided. But what was not composite was not severed; it remained inseparably in each. The proof that God was in the body is that the flesh was kept in incorruption after death, and incorruption is surely God. The proof that he did not leave the soul is that through it the way into paradise was opened for the thief. So when the mystery of death was fulfilled, the divine power had come to be in both parts of human nature. Through each it had placed its life-giving energy in the part akin to it: through the flesh in the body, and through the soul in the soul. I mean the rational soul, not the irrational one, for what lacks understanding is bestial, not human. Then the Godhead, which from the beginning had been blended with the body and the soul and had remained with them throughout, is raised in the resurrection of the one who lay dead. In this way Christ is said to have been raised from the dead. He himself both is Christ and became Christ. He is Christ by his kingship before the ages. He became Christ when the angels announced to the shepherds the great joy that would come to all the people at the birth of the Saviour, "who is," it says, "Christ the Lord." He is fittingly so named, in keeping with the word of Gabriel, who said that the Holy Spirit would come upon the Virgin and the power of the Most High would overshadow her. So the one born in this way is rightly called both Christ and Lord: Lord because of the power of the Most High, and Christ because of the Spirit of anointing. For it is not the one who is before the ages who is anointed at that time, but the one of whom it is said: "You are my Son; today I have begotten you." For "today" is the midpoint between the two divisions of time, the past and the future. But how could the maker of the ages be both begotten and anointed in a portion of time? So the Godhead has both not died and been raised. It has not died, because what is not composite is not dissolved. It has been raised, because, being present in what was dissolved, it caused the one who had fallen by the law of human nature to be lifted up together with itself. It was present to each part in the way proper to it, so that it might heal the nature of bodies through the body and the nature of souls through the soul. And again, having united in itself what had been separated, it rises in what is lifted up. Nothing prevents us from illustrating the mystery of the dispensation of the resurrection in bodily terms. Suppose a reed were split in two, and someone joined the tips of the two pieces together at one end. Then the whole of one piece would necessarily be fitted to the whole of the other, joined to the other piece through the meeting and binding at that one end. In the same way the union of soul and body that came about in him… [Editor's notes: (42) Read: "but the non-composite was not separated, but remained inseparably." (43) Read: "in the body."
