…through the resurrection brings the whole of human nature into one continuous natural unity, though death had split it in two, into soul and body. By the hope of resurrection it fits back together what had been parted. This is what Paul says: "Christ has been raised from the dead, the first fruits of those who have fallen asleep; and as in Adam we all die, so in Christ we shall all be made alive." For, following the example of the reed, at the end that is Adam our nature was split through sin, as death separated the soul from the body. But from the part that is Christ, the nature recovers itself again, and the division grows back together completely in the resurrection of the man in Christ. For this reason we die with the one who died for us. I do not mean the necessary death common to our nature, for that will happen to us even against our will. But since those who wish to die with the one who died voluntarily must do so willingly, they ought to find a death they choose, for what is forced cannot imitate what is voluntary. The death that lies upon each of us by nature comes in any case and by all means, whether we will it or not, and no one could count as voluntary what happens in any case. So we die with the one who died voluntarily in another way: we are buried in the mystical water through baptism. "For we were buried with him," it says, "through baptism into death," so that the imitation of the resurrection may follow the imitation of death. But let us move on to the next part of his argument. "How," he says, "does God become man without being changed from being God, unless he became mind in a man?" Did he then understand [?] what he was saying? He says the Divine is unchangeable, and he is right to say so, for what is always the same by nature cannot become something other than what it is. But… [Editor's notes: (51) Read "willingly." (53) The text originally read "follow" without the prefix.]

…is the human mind equal to the Godhead, if, as Apollinarius says, the divine nature became the mind of a man? Suppose human nature receives in the same way either our mind or, in place of the mind, God. Then the two would be of equal size and equal weight, if the Godhead were contained in the same space as the mind. Compare someone measuring grain or some other seed into an empty vessel. No one would say that what fills the same measure differs in quantity from the other. Wheat is equal to spelt when, after one kind of seed has been emptied out of the bushel, the other fills it in its turn. So if the Godhead takes the place of the mind, no one could say that the Godhead is greater than the mind, since human nature contains it in the same way. Then there are two possibilities. Either the mind is equal to the Godhead, as Apollinarius would have it, and he was not altered in passing from the one to the other. Or the mind is inferior to the Divine, and in becoming the one from the other he was altered toward what is meaner. But who does not know that everything conceived in creation stands equally below the inaccessible and unapproachable nature? The change is therefore the same whether one says the Divine was changed into a creature or into a mind. Now if Apollinarius does not think it a change to come to be in a mind, nor to be mingled with the man without a mind, he testifies that the one who was blended was unaltered. And if he was not altered in becoming flesh, much more did he remain unchanged when he blended himself with the mind. But if Apollinarius charges that coming to be in a mind is a change, then taking the flesh as his own certainly does not escape the charge of alteration either. He goes on to say (I pass over what lies between): "If after the resurrection he became God and is no longer man, how will the Son of Man send his angels? And how shall we see the Son of Man coming on the clouds? And how, before he was united and deified, does he say, 'I and the Father are one'?" He goes through these points to establish that the nature of the body was in no way transformed into something more divine. On his account, the hair, the nails, the form, the shape and the outline of his bulk are still about him, and… [Editor's notes: (60) Apparently read "and this." (61) Read the accusative: "the inaccessible and unapproachable nature."]

…the rest: that is, all the parts of the body, both visible and hidden. For my part, I think it superfluous to argue that one ought not to have such earthbound and grovelling thoughts about God, since my opponent's own argument proclaims its absurdity by itself. But so that he may not suppose the divine oracles support his mythmaking, I will run briefly through each of his points. He says that at the consummation of all things the one who sends the angels is called Son of Man. For this reason he thinks we must believe that he remains in human properties forever. He does not remember the words of the Gospel, where in many places the Lord, in his own sayings, called the God over all a man. "There was a man, a householder," who let out the vineyard to tenants. After his servants had been killed, he also sent his only-begotten son, whom the tenants threw out of the vineyard and killed. Who was that man who sent the only-begotten? And who was the son who was killed outside the vineyard? And the one who held the wedding feast for his son: was he not himself given a human form by the Word? This too must be said [?]. The Lord was helping the weakness of those who despised a nature of the same form as their own and so could not believe in his Godhead. He wanted to tighten the slackness of their minds by fear and so brace them for faith. That is why he says that the Son of Man sends the angels at the judgment: so that the expectation of terrors might cure their unbelief toward what they saw. "But you will see," he says, "the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory." This too agrees with what has already been explained, whether it refers to that man who planted the vineyard and held the wedding feast for his son, or is taken in the sense already given. The saying is entirely free of Apollinarius's lowly supposition, and it does not suggest that we think of him in any bodily way. This is clearly shown by what is added to the saying that announces his appearing at the end of the ages: that the Lord will be seen by creation in the glory of his Father. From this it follows that there are two possibilities. Either we must think that the Father too has a human form, so that the Son, appearing in human shape, may appear in the Father's glory. Or, if the majesty of the Father's glory is free of every form seen in a shape, then the one who promised to be seen in the Father's glory does not take a human shape either. For the glory of a man is one thing, and the glory of the God over all is another. "But," he says, "through… [Editor's notes: (69) Read "and whatever is hidden." (72) Perhaps read "I will run over." (76) Read "from what has been said." (77) Read the indicative "is pure."]

…the flesh, speaking to men, he said, 'I and the Father are one.'" What folly, to think it proves that his appearing will afterwards be human that the Lord, speaking through flesh, said he was one with the Father! By this argument he is certainly establishing that the Father too lives precisely in flesh. The one who said he was one with the Father meant the unity to be understood. If it is understood not in the spiritual sense but in the human sense, as Apollinarius thinks, then the Father is exactly what the Son was then seen to be as a man. But the Divine is beyond every bodily notion. Therefore the union of the Son with the Father was not according to the human shape, but according to their communion in the divine nature and power. That this is so is made especially clear by what he says to Philip: "Whoever has seen me has seen the Father." For an accurate understanding of the Son's majesty lets one see the archetype, as in an image. I will pass over the incoherent and unintelligible passages that follow, so as not to linger idly over vanities. In them he does not even make clear what he means to say to those who follow his writing attentively. I cannot see what bearing it has on his argument that no one snatches out of his hand the sheep given him by the Father, or that he draws the sheep to himself by the Father's Godhead. He also says: "If Christ was united with the Father before the resurrection, how is he not united with the God in him?" He adds this to his own arguments as if he meant to refute his own mythmaking, for it demonstrates both the distinction and the union of the man with the Divine. Whoever says, "If Christ is united with the Father, how is he not united with the God in him?" implies that in the same way the man in Christ, being distinct, is united with the God in him. Since these points expose the error and incoherence of his doctrine as soon as they are read, I will pass over them in my discourse. I shall mention only this. "The Saviour," he says, "suffered hunger, thirst, weariness, agony and grief." Who is the Saviour? "God," he says in an earlier passage, "not two persons, as though God were one and the man another." So God suffered the things he says he suffered. And he says that what cannot admit suffering suffers, "not by necessity of an unwilling [?] nature, as a man does, but by the consequence of nature." Who could ever refute all these vanities? In what way does he see the necessity of nature as different from the consequence of nature? Truth sees the same meaning in both. Here is an example of what I mean:

"It follows that one whose eyes are not healthy has weak sight." And again I say the same thing: "It is necessary that, if someone's eyes are not healthy, his sight is weak." Is it not the same in both cases? The one who spoke of necessity pointed to what happens as a consequence, and the one who mentioned consequence signified what is necessary. What, then, does this learned writer mean by attributing the passions of nature to the Saviour "not by necessity of nature but by consequence of nature"? "It was needful," he says, "that the passions be stirred in the likeness of men." In saying "it was needful," has he not plainly declared necessity? Is this not also how Scripture uses the words? Proofs of this can be taken from the Gospels themselves: "It is necessary that stumbling blocks come"; and "for these things must take place." Do the two expressions not have one meaning? The one who said it is necessary that stumbling blocks come showed by these words that they must come. And the one who said, "These things must take place," foretold what had to come to pass by necessity. But again I will pass over the next piece of drivel, heaped together carelessly and at random out of vain reasonings. Toward the end of his treatise he says: "And while the body is in heaven, he is with us until the consummation of the age." The writer plainly divides the indivisible and does not understand who it is that is with us. If he places the body in heaven but says that the Lord is with us, this distinction clearly creates a separation and a division. He did not say that his body both remains in heaven and is with us. He said "while the body is in heaven" (and we are not in heaven). So he has come to believe that something other than the body in heaven is with us who are on earth. Such are the wise teachings of Apollinarius. But we say that after saying these things he was taken up, and the one who was taken up is with us, and there is no division in him. Just as he is in us, present to each and standing in our midst, so he also pervades all the ends of creation and shows himself equally in every part of the world… [Editor's notes: (83) Read "Is this not also Scripture's usage?" …he mingles himself with men. Toward the end of his treatise he gasps out [?] a number of things, as if in fits of breathlessness, held fast by insubstantial notions.

I think these should be passed over without examination. In them, hard pressed, he calls on the Greeks to defend his own myths. As for the other passages like these, anyone who wants to see how feeble the heresy is throughout may go through the writings themselves. But we do not have so much leisure as to spend time on such arguments, which make their own absurdity plain even before they are examined. [?]
